name: DLR-FT wasm-interpreter
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift), Wasmer (Cranelift) startup
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup suite: compile + instantiate of 7 modules from tiny to huge, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Startup geomean on AMD EPYC 7763 relative to the per-case fastest runtime (lower is better): DLR-wasm-interpreter x10.95 versus Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1634.19, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1484.15, Wasmtime (Winch) x298.15, Wasmer (Singlepass) x162.12 and V8 x33.27; about 149x faster startup than Wasmtime (Cranelift) and 136x faster than Wasmer (Cranelift) (derived from page data). Per case in the raw data (wasmi-benchmarks data/amd-epyc-7763/criterion.json, criterion typical estimate): coremark 62.7 us vs 9.87 ms, ffmpeg 127.1 ms vs 17.96 s for Wasmtime (Cranelift).
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks (github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks) Cargo.toml [profile.bench] lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, run as 'cargo criterion --bench criterion --all-features ... startup/' (criterion 0.8.2; sample_size 10, 2 s measurement, 1 s warm-up). Rust toolchain: .github/workflows/startup.yml uses dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable with no rust-toolchain file, so the rustc version is not recorded; the C/C++ runtimes are built with gcc-15/g++-15 (.github/actions/install-dependencies). Runtime versions are pinned only by the Cargo.lock at HEAD (wasmtime 47.0.3, wasmer 7.2.1); the plots repo does not record which suite commit produced them.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (plot title and data/amd-epyc-7763 directory). This is the CPU of GitHub's ubuntu-latest runners and the suite's startup.yml workflow runs there, so the data probably come from a shared CI VM (not confirmed). The plots repo also holds Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C data, not read here.
tradeoffs: In-place interpretation of WebAssembly 2.0 with no intermediate representation, no_std, aimed at avionics; no GC proposal planned.
caveats: The suite is maintained and run by the Wasmi author, so it is third-party for every runtime except Wasmi. Ratios were read from the SVG text labels and checked against the raw criterion data, which reproduce the startup geomeans exactly. The measured crate is dlr-wasm-interpreter 0.2.0 (current crates.io release). Startup is decode + validate + instantiate of 7 modules (erc20 to ffmpeg); the win is an in-place interpreter versus optimizing JITs, which is expected. Against other interpreters it is not the fastest: Wasmi v2 lazy-translation (also validates eagerly) is x10.66, Wasmi v2 lazy x1.37 and Wasm3 lazy x2.77, and V8 starts faster on the two largest modules (ffmpeg 35.5 ms vs 127.1 ms, spidermonkey 10.9 ms vs 32.9 ms). Startup-only win: execution geomean on the same CPU (plot geomean-execute.svg) is x122.00, about 7 times slower than WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07 (derived from page data), over 20 of 21 cases (no tail calls); the committed criterion.json gives a different execute geomean (98.25), so the execute plot came from another run. Data probably from a shared GitHub Actions VM. The project's own README gives no performance numbers.

name: Fizzy
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift), Wasmer (Cranelift) startup
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup suite: compile + instantiate of 7 modules from tiny to huge, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Startup (compile plus instantiate) geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test (lower is better), AMD EPYC 7763: Fizzy x17.83 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x56.73, V8 x33.27, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1484.15, Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1634.19 (about 3.2x lower than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data). Fizzy is below WAMR fast-interp on all five CPU data sets (Apple M2 Pro 18.69 vs 49.35, Apple M4 Pro 17.20 vs 43.90, Intel i7-7700 17.63 vs 61.71, Xeon Platinum 8573C 11.21 vs 44.15) and below V8 on four of them, but not on Apple M2 Pro (Fizzy 18.69 vs V8 16.97).
compiler_and_flags: Built by the wasmi-benchmarks harness through Robin Freyler's fizzyx 0.1.1 crate: fizzyx-sys build.rs runs Fizzy's CMake via the Rust cmake crate with FIZZY_TESTING=OFF, FIZZY_WASI=OFF and a force-included compat_shim.hpp; Rust harness profile.bench lto=fat, codegen-units=1. C++ compiler, version and CMake build type are not stated. Fizzy's own README performance setup: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (-O3), LTO, latest GCC or Clang, libstdc++, no -march=native.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: WebAssembly 1.0 only; supports no GC, SIMD or newer proposals. Built for deterministic blockchain use (metering, canonical floating point).
caveats: Startup-only win: on the same suite Fizzy's execution geomean is x45.63 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51 and V8 x1.05 on EPYC 7763 (about 2.7x slower than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data), so it is not faster than any category baseline at running code. Per-test startup on EPYC: V8 is faster than Fizzy on ffmpeg (35.46 ms vs 215.36 ms), spidermonkey (10.94 ms vs 52.31 ms) and pulldown-cmark (2.30 ms vs 2.72 ms); Fizzy wins on bz2, coremark, argon2 and erc20. Lazy-validating interpreters are far faster at startup (Wasm3 lazy x2.77, Wasmi v2 lazy x1.37). The WAMR comparison is against its fast-interpreter mode, which precompiles at load. Suite is maintained by the author of the competing Wasmi runtime and the Fizzy bindings (fizzyx) are his; plots are regenerated in place (last EPYC update 2026-08-25, values as of 2026-10-06). Fizzy implements WebAssembly 1.0 (MVP) only. Latest commit (2025-11-10) is a README merge; the last code change was 2023-03-03. Fizzy's own CHANGELOG (v0.5.0 detailed results, hardware not stated) shows execution about 5.1x faster than WABT 1.0.19 interpreter (508%) but only 1.7x faster than WABT 1.0.12 (167%), while wasm3 0.4.7 took 26% of Fizzy's execution time and 27% of its instantiation time. Fizzy failed in Frank Denis's libsodium 2021-Q1 run (needs WASI poll_oneoff).

name: Silverfir-nano
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (execution) and Wasmtime Cranelift (startup)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks execution suite: 22 cases (counters, fibonacci, sort, nbody, argon2, json-parse, regex-redux and others), geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Execution geomean on AMD EPYC 7763 relative to the per-case fastest runtime (lower is better): Silverfir-nano interpreter x9.02 versus WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51 and Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92 (about 1.9x faster than WAMR, derived from page data); Silverfir-nano JIT x1.25, close to but not beating Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1.15, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1.17 and V8 x1.05; Wasmtime (Winch) is x2.35 and Wasmer (Singlepass) x2.95.
compiler_and_flags: Guests: wasi-sdk clang (version not stated) -O2 --target=wasm32-wasip1 via benchmarks/wasi/Makefile, binaries committed and shared by all engines. Silverfir: cargo --release, workspace profile lto=true, codegen-units=1, opt-level=3. wasmtime Cranelift and Winch 47.0.2 built from source with rustc 1.97.0; Node 25.9.0 (V8 14.1.146); wasm3 '~/Dev/wasm3 build-release' (commit and flags not stated); wasmi_cli 2.0.0-beta.7 via cargo install (CoreMark cell 2.0.0-beta.10). Harness: benchmarks/wasi/run_tests.py and run_v8.mjs.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: Ships both an interpreter and an on-device optimizing JIT; no_std; targets six ISAs from x86_64 and ARM64 down to RV32 and Thumb-2. Binary 337 KiB with the interpreter and 1,042 KiB with the JIT (README, RP2350 firmware).
caveats: First-party suite, one machine (M4), interpreters are single runs (author says treat as +/-5%) while compiled engines are the mean of two rounds; Cranelift still wins 9 of 15 metrics and is ahead on sqlite and LZ4 decompress (3,478 vs 3,241), so the JIT claim is parity, not a win. Wasmtime 47.0.2 and V8 14.1 are older than current releases (wasmtime v49 was current in September 2026); the numbers are dated 2026-07-24/25 and share no baseline with earlier revisions of the file. CoreMark runs in a non-standard bounded regression mode, except the interpreter CoreMark row, which was refreshed on 2026-08-31 with standalone scores and uses wasmi 2.0.0-beta.10 rather than beta.7. The wasm3 build compared against is not pinned to a version. The sqlite and Lua rows are historical (the active suite has changed those benchmarks). Independent cross-check in the wasmi-benchmarks suite (wasmi-labs, AMD EPYC 7763, plot raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg, date not stated, 23 runtime configurations): execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is Silverfir interpreter 9.02 vs Wasmi v2 12.40, Wasm3 16.51, WAMR fast-interp 17.07 and Pulley 27.92 (fastest interpreter, about 1.37x ahead of Wasmi v2, derived from page data), and Silverfir JIT 1.25 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15, Wasmer Cranelift 1.17 and V8 1.05, so the JIT trails the optimizing compilers slightly on that suite. That suite is run by the author of wasmi, a competing interpreter.

name: Stitch (makepad)
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter and Wasmtime Pulley (execution); Wasmtime Cranelift (startup)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks execution suite: 22 cases, geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Execution geomean on AMD EPYC 7763 relative to the per-case fastest runtime (lower is better): Stitch (lazy) x15.73 versus WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07 and Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92 (about 1.09x faster than WAMR, derived from page data); Wasm3 (eager) is x16.51, Wasmi v2 (eager) x12.40; Wasmtime (Cranelift) is x1.15.
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release in coremark/ (Rust release profile; rustc version not stated). Harness pins wasmi 0.31.2 and wasmtime 20.0.1; the wasm3 runner (wasm3 crate 0.3.1) is commented out in coremark/Cargo.toml and coremark/src/main.rs at HEAD.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: Relies on LLVM sibling-call optimization (not guaranteed) and a 64-bit target only; about 15k lines of code with significant unsafe and no external audit (README).
caveats: Only a single CoreMark workload; the edge over wasm3 is within a few percent on Mac and negative on Linux, and Wasmtime's JIT is 4-8x faster than Stitch, so it does not beat any JIT baseline in the category. The Wasmi baseline is the old 0.31.2 stack interpreter (open issue #2 asks for an update since Wasmi 0.32+ is much faster); the wasm3 runner is commented out of the published harness. Open correctness issues #3 and #4 (filed by the Wasmi author, July 2025 and June 2026): live locals and registers are not preserved on entering block/if/loop, so some modules return wrong results (example returns 0 instead of 42); unfixed upstream. Relies on LLVM sibling-call optimisation with no guarantee; 64-bit only; no SIMD or WASI; large amount of unaudited unsafe code (README). Independent wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks plots (Aug 2026; criterion, profile.bench lto=fat, codegen-units=1) measure a bug-fixed fork (Robbepop/stitch branch v0.1-dev, shown as 'Stitch (lazy)'): geomean execute time relative to the fastest runtime is Stitch 15.73 vs Wasm3 (eager) 16.51 on AMD EPYC 7763, 11.94 vs 12.64 on Apple M2 Pro, 9.70 vs 10.71 on Apple M4 Pro (about 1.05-1.10x faster than Wasm3, derived from page data), but Wasmi v2 (eager) is faster than Stitch on all three (12.40, 8.83, 8.06). The record's claim about rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark was not checked by the verifier.

name: wasm3
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (iwasm); Wasmtime Pulley interpreter; WasmEdge interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (xmrsplayer audio, AssemblyScript graphql, audio DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max (A12) E-cores.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime (lower is better), M4 Max E-cores: wasm3 1.01, WAMR fast-interp 1.63, Wasmtime Pulley 2.09, WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; A12 E-cores: wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68, WasmEdge 9.28. About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4 (derived from page data). Page text: 'wasm3 is the fastest interpreter on nearly every case it runs'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0 built with -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0), no WASI sources; WAMR cmake Release -O3 FAST_INTERP only (AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off); Pulley rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls, fat LTO
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Pure interpreter with no JIT or AOT tier: far slower than compiling runtimes. In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test is wasm3 16.51x vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x. Very cheap startup: same suite startup geomean wasm3 lazy 2.77x vs WAMR fast-interp 56.73x, V8 33.27x, Wasmer Cranelift 1484.15x, Wasmtime Cranelift 1634.19x. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the benchmark tested it supports only tail calls and extended-const. Maintainer states the project is in a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Result is interpreter versus interpreter: wasm3 is not faster than JIT/AOT Wasmtime, Wasmer or V8 (its own docs/Performance.md CoreMark table, 2019-2020 on an i5-8250U and labelled historical by the project, has wasmtime 0.8.0 and Wasmer Cranelift 4.0x faster and wasm-micro-runtime 8.1x slower; in the wasmi-benchmarks suite on an AMD EPYC 7763 its execute geomean is 16.51 vs Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15 and V8 1.05, and behind Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02 and Wasmi v2 12.40). The 17-case geomean covers only MVP/scalar code: wasm3 cannot run the SIMD-canonical builds, exceptions, GC, typed references, memory64 or multi-memory, and WAMR leads on the SIMD rows. Instantiation is its weak spot: extended-const modules cost it 116-122x Pulley's time on the M4 (62-85x on the A12). The benchmark author built WAMR with 29 carried patches, WasmEdge with 26 and Pulley from a fork branch with 9 extra commits, while wasm3 v0.9.0 ran unpatched. Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. Independent libsodium 2021-Q1 run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md): 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test', native about 30x faster than wasm3 and about 46x faster than WAMR. The README still declares a minimal maintenance phase, though September 2026 commits add atomics and an exception-handling API.

Startup ratios are dominated by lazy modes: 'lazy' defers both compilation and validation of function bodies to first use, so x1.37 skips work that Cranelift, Winch and V8 do eagerly; lazy-translation with eager validation (x10.66) and eager mode (x38.88) are fairer compile-cost comparisons, and eager Wasmi v2 is slower than V8 (x33.27) on startup. name: wasmz
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter and WAMR fast interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison of 7 runtimes on Apple Silicon E-cores: 17 shared cases, CPU time per call.
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geometric mean over 17 cases, N=10: Apple M4 Max E-cores wasmz 1.59 vs WAMR 1.63 and Pulley 2.09 (about 1.3x faster than Pulley, derived from page data); iPhone XS (A12) E-cores wasmz 1.63 vs Pulley 1.68 but WAMR 1.38.
compiler_and_flags: wasmz dev built with 'make release' (Zig ReleaseFast); wasm3 at submodule commit 79d412e built with cmake (its CMakeLists defaults to Release, -O3); WAMR at submodule commit 11eb206 built with cmake -DWAMR_BUILD_INTERP=1 -DWAMR_BUILD_AOT=0 -DWAMR_BUILD_FAST_JIT=0 -DWAMR_BUILD_JIT=0 -DWAMR_BUILD_SIMD=0; wasmi at commit 9f6ff82 built with cargo build --release -p wasmi_cli (all in bench/build.sh). Compiler versions (Zig, gcc, rustc) are not stated in the report.
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (E-cores) and iPhone XS Max (Apple A12 Bionic, E-cores)
tradeoffs: Zig library with C API and Rust bindings; GC, SIMD, exceptions and threads claimed.
caveats: First-party numbers from a 2026-04-16 dev build; CPU model and compiler versions not stated. The wasm3 used is v0.5.1 (submodule commit 79d412e); the independent harness used v0.9.0. Timings are whole-process wall time via hyperfine, so start-up is included and wasmz's lazy (on first call) compilation favours it on the 19 MB esbuild module; WAMR is excluded from esbuild. The harness does not check program output. Many miscompilation fixes landed after the benchmark (August 2026 commits such as 'keep operand-stack reads of a local independent of later writes' and 'only rename a label slot onto the temporary that a branch consumes'), so the numbers were measured on code later fixed for correctness bugs. The QuickJS and esbuild memory rows measure the sh -c wrapper (1.8 MB for every runtime), so those RSS figures are invalid. The independent harness rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, wasmz v0.1.4) puts wasmz behind wasm3 (geomean 1.59 vs 1.01 on M4 Max E-cores). It is roughly level with WAMR fast-interp there (1.63) but behind it on iPhone XS A12 (1.63 vs 1.38), and ahead of wasmtime Pulley (2.09). The same harness reports six failing rows for wasmz: wrong results on extconst_init and extconst_init.mvp, traps on graphql_as and callref_dispatch, and segfaults on v128 ops in sieve and crc32. It also notes that wasmz never collects GC structs and does not support multi-memory or multi-value results through its C API. Treat the win over WAMR and wasm3 as unconfirmed. Zig library with a C API (libwasmz plus wasmz.h), so callable from C++.

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR)
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter (A-tier numbers); Wasmtime, Wasmer and V8 JIT/AOT (libsodium suite)
workload: Interpreter-only comparison on the 17 Wasm cases every runtime runs (audio, graphql, DSP, MVP kernels), CPU time per call, N=10 per platform, Apple M4 Max E-cores and iPhone XS Max E-cores; WAMR configured as fast interpreter only.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime over the 17 cases all seven runtimes run (lower is better): M4 Max E-cores WAMR fast-interp 1.63 vs Wasmtime Pulley 2.09 and WasmEdge interpreter 8.42; iPhone XS (A12) E-cores 1.38 vs 1.68 and 9.28. About 1.28x faster than Pulley on the M4 and 1.22x on the A12 (derived from page data). Per case on M4 (CPU ms per call): bulk_memory 10.41 vs 22.14, call_indirect 18.48 vs 31.53, convolution 3.928 vs 5.883, sieve 0.5128 vs 0.7082. The harness repo's earlier docs/cross-runtime-pulley-vs-wamr.md (iPhone 12, 2026-05-15, Pulley with the author's phase-3 fusion patches) has WAMR 1.37-1.86x faster on call_indirect, xmrsplayer, graphql (AssemblyScript) and the vtable suite.
compiler_and_flags: WAMR main (WAMR-2.4.1-364, b70d708d, 2026-09-21) with 29 local patches, cmake Release -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12, INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 BULK_MEMORY=1 TAIL_CALL=1 etc., WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1; Pulley from wasmtime v49 fork (9 extra commits), rust nightly-2026-07-05, RUSTFLAGS --cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12, fat LTO, 1 CGU; Apple clang 21.0.0 (Xcode 27.0).
hardware: Apple M4 Max E-cores (MacBook Pro, macOS 27.0); iPhone XS Max A12 Bionic E-cores (iOS 18.7.10)
tradeoffs: Configurable runtime (classic and fast interpreter, AOT via wamrc, Fast JIT, LLVM JIT); README lists small text sizes on cortex-m4f (about 58.9K fast interpreter, 56.3K classic interpreter, 29.4K AOT runtime). The fast interpreter is slower than wasm3 (1.63x vs 1.01x in the cited doc).
caveats: WAMR is itself a category baseline; listed for its measured wins over Wasmtime's Pulley interpreter and, in AOT mode, over JIT runtimes. The win is interpreter versus interpreter, not versus Wasmtime's native Cranelift JIT. Pulley is not ahead everywhere: it beats WAMR on fib (1.13 vs 1.38 relative on M4), fib_tail, tailcall_fsm and extconst_init. In the same harness WAMR is slower than wasm3 (1.63 vs 1.01 geomean) and level with wasmz (1.59 on M4, 1.63 on A12). The benchmarked WAMR is unreleased main (the latest release, 2.4.5, lacks 364 of those commits) carrying 29 patches by the benchmark author (legacy EH, relaxed SIMD, PROT_NONE linear memory), and the Pulley side is a fork with 9 extra commits (including call_indirect argument bundling). Only Apple Silicon E-cores measured. AOT evidence (derived from page data, reproduced by the verifier): in jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2022-12 libsodium CSVs (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2022-12/res/iwasm.csv with wasmtime.csv, wasmer-cranelift.csv, wasmer-llvm.csv, node.csv, native.csv) the iwasm geomean time over the 61 tests common to all six files is 0.665x Wasmtime, 0.688x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.794x Wasmer LLVM and 0.588x Node/V8, and 2.30x native; the CSVs do not say iwasm ran in AOT mode (inferred from magnitude; CPU and flags not in the repo, and no README for that run). In the wasmi-benchmarks suite (AMD EPYC 7763, execute geomean relative to the fastest runtime per test, date not stated) WAMR fast-interp is 17.07 vs Pulley 27.92, but behind Wasm3 16.51, Wasmz 15.89, Wasmi v2 12.40 and Silverfir-nano's interpreter 9.02. WAMR wiki (https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/wiki/Performance, i7-7700, GCC 7.5.0 -O3, 2020-09-01) compares only against wasm3 and native.

name: zwasm
baseline: wasmtime 43.0.1; wasmer 5.0.4; wazero 1.11.0; WasmEdge 0.16.1 (interpreter)
workload: End-to-end wall time of '<runtime> run <module>' (spawn, instantiate, execute WASI _start) with hyperfine on short TinyGo and ClojureWasm guests, plus peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
claimed_speedup: Startup-bound short workloads (mean ms): tinygo/fib zwasm-aot 2.0, interp 2.3, jit 2.8 vs wasmtime 7.2, wazero 7.1, wasmer 12.0, WasmEdge 16.5. Peak RSS on tinygo/fib: zwasm-aot 2.1 MB, jit 3.2, interp 2.7 vs wazero 8.7, wasmtime 13.3, WasmEdge 23.7, wasmer 27.5 ('4-12x less').
compiler_and_flags: zwasm built with Zig 0.16.0 (pinned in flake.nix) via zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; comparators wasmtime 43.0.1, wazero 1.11.0, wasmer 5.0.4, WasmEdge 0.16.1 pinned in flake.nix devShells.bench; hyperfine 5 runs plus 3 warmup; peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (Mac aarch64), one host
tradeoffs: Single-pass JIT, interpreter and AOT backends with Wasm 3.0 and WASI 0.2/0.3; small footprint and fast startup traded for peak throughput.
caveats: The win is cold-start latency and memory footprint only. The same doc shows the optimizing JITs ahead on sustained compute: wasmtime/wasmer/wazero beat zwasm-jit/aot by about 1.5-3.9x (shootout/fib2 zwasm-jit 1077 ms vs wasmtime 700 ms; matrix 343 vs 88 ms; base64 781 vs 57 ms, about 13.7x). The startup rows time a whole process (spawn + instantiate + run) on sub-10 ms guests, so they measure startup, not execution; the zwasm-aot row excludes its one-off compile step while comparator rows include their JIT compile, and the doc does not say whether wasmtime/wasmer compilation caches were on. Single host (Apple M4 Pro, macOS); wasmer only on aarch64-darwin. The independent harness at rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (docs/runtime-comparison-2026-09-22.md, zwasm v2.7.0 with the JIT compiled out) puts zwasm's interpreter at a geomean 8.47x the fastest runtime's CPU time on M4 Max E-cores (wasm3 1.01, WAMR 1.63, WasmEdge 8.42). A fork's README (andypeng2015/zwasm) says the 'majority match or beat wasmtime' on 29 benchmarks, which the canonical benchmarks doc does not support. github.com/clojurewasm/zwasm (used by the rebecker harness) appears to be the project's earlier home. v1 line (frozen at v1.11.1) is MIT; v2 is Apache-2.0. Embeddable from C/C++ via the standard wasm-c-api.

name: wasm2c (WABT)
baseline: Wasmtime, Wasmer (Cranelift, LLVM, Singlepass) and V8 (Node.js)
workload: libsodium benchmark suite, 2022-12 run: 61 tests with results for every listed runtime plus native; wasm2c translates Wasm to C which is then compiled natively.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (wasm2c.csv vs the other runtimes' CSVs, geomean of per-test time ratios over the 61 tests that have native results): wasm2c 0.68x Wasmtime, 0.71x Wasmer Cranelift, 0.82x Wasmer LLVM, 0.61x Node/V8, 0.22x Wasmer Singlepass; wasm2c geomean 2.36x native vs Wasmtime 3.46x, Wasmer Cranelift 3.34x, Wasmer LLVM 2.89x, Node 3.91x. Not faster than WAMR: iwasm (AOT per the 2023 post, snippet only) is 2.30x native, wasm2c 1.03x iwasm time, slower on 31 of 61 tests.
stars_or_usage: 8.1k stars (WABT toolkit; wasm2c is one tool in it)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time only: the generated C must be compiled by a C compiler per module, so no JIT and an extra build step. Optional Segue optimisation (Linux x86-64, clang with -mfsgsbase) and optional extra sanity checks (WASM_RT_SANITY_CHECKS, high overhead, meant for debug builds) are described in wasm2c/README.md.
caveats: Not a win over every category baseline: in the same 2022-12 run WAMR iwasm (AOT-compiled per the 00f.net 2023 post, search snippet only) is at par or slightly ahead (wasm2c 1.03x iwasm time geomean over 61 tests, wasm2c slower on 31 of them; iwasm 2.30x native vs wasm2c 2.36x, derived from page data). The results repo (archived 2026-08-19) has no compiler, flags or CPU model for the 2022-12 run (methodology lives in the blocked 00f.net post) and the CSV unit is not stated; lower is better (native lowest, wasm3 highest), so only ratios are used. The native column uses hardware AES on the AEGIS tests (about 74x faster than any Wasm runtime there), which inflates every runtime's x-native geomean equally. Frank Denis's 2026 post (search snippet only, 00f.net blocked) reports wasm2c built with zig cc -O3 -march=native at 0.814x Wasmtime and 0.887x Wasmer geomean with wide_arithmetic, and WAMR AOT at about 1.57x native. The wasm2c C-compile step is not part of the measured time, and the C compiler and flags used to build the wasm2c output in 2022-12 are not public.

name: WasmEdge

name: aWsm
baseline: Wasmer; WAVM; Lucet; Node.js with Emscripten; wasm3 on microcontrollers
workload: PolyBench/C slowdown over native C, on x86-64, aarch64 (Raspberry Pi) and Cortex-M4/M7, for an ahead-of-time Wasm-to-LLVM compiler with a small C runtime.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 average slowdown over native: Wasmer 149.8%, WAVM 28.1%, Node.js + Emscripten 84.0%, Lucet 92.8%, aWsm 13.4%. aarch64: aWsm 6.7%. Cortex-M7 40.2% and M4 24.9%, versus 'more than 10x' for the wasm3 interpreter on microcontrollers (links wasm3's Performance.md).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the cross-runtime comparison. The repo's code_benches/run.py (native vs aWsm only) builds native code with clang -O3 and Wasm with wasi-sdk/wasmception clang -O3 -flto, then compiles aWsm's LLVM bitcode with clang -O3.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler through LLVM, so compile latency; the runtime is under 5K lines of C and the compiler under 3.5K lines of Rust; output is ELF objects; seven selectable memory-bounds-check mechanisms. Not a fit where interpreters or JIT are required.
caveats: README says 'these numbers are from May 2020'; hardware, compiler versions and flags are not given in the README. A search snippet (snippet only) says the Middleware 2020 Sledge paper holds the same x86-64 comparison with Wasmer v0.12.0, WAVM v0.0.0-prerelease and Lucet v0.4.1, and that aWsm is within 1.1x of native on 24 of 30 PolyBench/C kernels; the paper itself was not reachable (a paper-access retier could move this to B). Wasmtime is absent from the x86-64 table, and all comparator versions are 2020-era. Microcontroller support: Arm's bento-linker README (an Arm collaborator of the aWsm group) measures aWsm on an nRF52840 (Cortex-M4, arm-none-eabi-gcc -Os -flto -mcpu=cortex-m4, compiler version not stated) at 78,896 ns vs 132,688 ns for WAMR AOT and 2,079,359 ns for wasm3 on qsort, and 6,823,538 ns vs 12,368,716 ns (WAMR AOT) and 157,946,032 ns (wasm3) on maze. Rust compiler plus C runtime: only the generated objects and runtime are linked into C/C++ programs. The 2026-07-13 last commit is a submodule bump; the previous code change was 2025-11-19 and the README pins Rust 1.56.0, so development is slow.

name: LFI (Lightweight Fault Isolation)
baseline: WebAssembly ahead-of-time engines: WAMR 1.2.2 (LLVM AOT), Wasm2c 1.0.33 + Clang (with UVWASI), Wasmtime 16.0.0 (Cranelift AOT); all relative to native code compiled with LTO
workload: Run-time overhead versus native code compiled with LTO on SPEC CPU2017 single-copy rate C/C++ benchmarks (14 for LFI; the 7 that build under WASI for the Wasm comparison), Arm64 only in the paper, for in-process software sandboxing compared with WebAssembly AOT sandboxing.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2024 paper Table 4, geomean run-time overhead over native LTO code on the 7 SPEC CPU2017 rate benchmarks that build for WASI: LFI 7.3% (GCP T2A) / 6.4% (Apple M1) vs WAMR 22.3% / 18.2%, Wasm2c 40.7% / 37.5% (16.5% / 15.7% after the paper's barrier removal and pinned heap register), Wasmtime 47.0% / 67.1%. Derived from page data: LFI-sandboxed code runs about 1.14x (T2A) / 1.11x (M1) faster than WAMR AOT, about 1.09x faster than the tuned Wasm2c, and 1.37x / 1.57x faster than Wasmtime. Over all 14 supported SPEC benchmarks LFI O2 overhead is 6.4% (M1) and 7.3% (T2A), about 1% when loads are not sandboxed. Repo README at HEAD: 7% (Arm64) / 8% (x86-64) overhead for read and write sandboxing, 1.5% / 6% for writes only (geomean SPEC 2017); lfi-research README: LLVM-based AOT Wasm compilers 'incur upwards of 20% runtime overhead'.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM/Clang 15.0.7 with the LFI rewriter for native, LFI and Wasm builds; Wasm bytecode further optimized with wasm-opt, SIMD128 enabled, bounds checks replaced by guard pages; Wasmtime run in AOT mode. Per-benchmark SPEC compile flags are in the artifact's cpu2017/config files (paper text does not list them; artifact not opened).
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Air 3.2 GHz (Asahi Linux 6.3.0); Google Cloud T2A instance 3.0 GHz (Linux 6.1.0)
tradeoffs: Sandboxes native C/C++/assembly rather than Wasm bytecode: no stable binary format, no platform independence, Arm64 and x86-64 only (RISC-V experimental); needs an LFI compiler toolchain and a verifier; ~64K (Arm64) or ~3K (x86-64) sandboxes of up to 4 GiB per address space.
caveats: Different execution model from a Wasm VM: LFI sandboxes native code recompiled with its own LLVM toolchain and replaces Wasm rather than running Wasm faster. Paper numbers are Arm64 only and were measured on the original research implementation (lfi-research branch, MPL-2.0; repo HEAD is MIT and the code now lives in sibling repos lfi-runtime, lfi-rewriter, lfi-verifier after submodules were removed in January 2026). The x86-64 figures (8% and 6%) in the HEAD README have no linked measurement; the lfi-research README gave ~9-10% for x86-64. In the paper WAMR and the modified Wasm2c were run as non-conforming Wasm implementations (no trap-semantics compiler barrier), only 7 of 14 benchmarks could be compared with Wasm, and SPEC CPU2017 is a licensed suite so reproduction needs a SPEC licence (artifact offers CoreMark as an alternative). Research project; x86-64 verifier was incomplete in the research version.

name: UWVM2 (u2 interpreter)
baseline: wasm3
workload: Wall time of 383 .wasm modules that both uwvm2's u2 interpreter and wasm3 could run, plus WASI algorithm kernels (ChaCha20, SHA512, BLAKE2s), on AArch64 Apple Silicon.
claimed_speedup: Wall-time ratio uwvm/wasm3 geomean 0.5957 over n=383 modules (u2 faster on average), median 0.7116; ChaCha20 398ms vs 515ms, SHA512 202ms vs 220ms, BLAKE2s 3094ms vs 3427ms (internal time).
hardware: AArch64 Apple M-series (exact chip not stated)
tradeoffs: Template-specialized opfuncs trade code size for speed (Mach-O __TEXT about 1.4 MB), so u2 is not a minimal wasm3-class interpreter. C++26 codebase. Tiered interpreter + JIT design; supports many platforms, WASI P1, and mmap or allocator-based linear memory.
caveats: First-party section 9.1 of the u2 interpreter README, labelled by the authors as 'not universal claims', from a 2026-02 AArch64/Apple Silicon workflow with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated. The 383-module corpus lives in /tmp/uwvm2test and is not published; the cited analysis note test/uwvm2test/u2_vs_wasm3_asm_stitch_analysis.txt returns 404 and the repo's test/ directory has no uwvm2test folder; benchmark/ only covers parser and utility code. The README says memory-heavy and branch-heavy kernels can lose to wasm3 and that u2 trades code size for speed (not a minimal interpreter in the wasm3/WAMR class). Translation-time peepholes that delete const+drop runs and inline trivial calls could flatter microbenchmark modules in the corpus. Not compared with wasmtime, wasmer or WAMR; wasm3 is the only baseline.

name: VMIR
baseline: LLVM lli (LLVM IR interpreter)
workload: test/misc/src/sha1test.c over 64MB of random data, run as LLVM bitcode in the VMIR interpreter versus lli.
claimed_speedup: Core i7 3.2GHz, sha1test over 64MB of random data: VMIR 4.8s vs LLVM LLI 7m 39s (about 96x faster, derived from page data); native 0.39s (VMIR about 12x slower than native, derived from page data). Raspberry Pi 2 (BCM2709): VMIR 1m 42s, VMIR JIT 17.5s, native 3.54s (no LLI figure). README: interpretation is about 10x slower than native on x86.
hardware: Core i7 3.2GHz (exact model not stated); ARMv7 BCM2709 (Raspberry Pi 2): VMIR 1m42s, VMIR JIT 17.5s, native 3.54s
tradeoffs: Standalone C library that executes both LLVM bitcode (.bc) and WebAssembly (.wasm); the built-in libc is incomplete, no vector types, no C++ STL support, and the JIT exists only for 32-bit ARM and does not cover all instruction classes.
caveats: Single README table, one workload (SHA-1), no exact CPU model, no LLVM version or lli flags, and no statement of which bitcode optimisation level (the test Makefile builds -O0, -O1 and -O2) was timed. The 96x gap is against lli's interpreter, which the README itself says 'is not intended to run code fast in any way', so it is a weak baseline; against native code VMIR is about 12x slower on x86 and about 29x slower on the Pi 2 (JIT about 5x slower; derived from page data). The JIT exists only for 32-bit ARM. VMIR also runs WebAssembly but is not compared with wasm3, WAMR or wasmtime. Built-in libc is incomplete, no vector types (code must be compiled with -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize), no C++ STL. Last commit 2018-08-29.

name: w2c2
baseline: Wasmtime (independent blog runs); native C for the README CoreMark figure
workload: README: CoreMark 1.0 translated by w2c2 and compiled to C, against native CoreMark (examples/coremark). Wasmtime comparisons: an unnamed module in Frank Denis's 2023-12-11 post and CoreMark in Andy Wingo's 2025-10-30 Wastrel post (both blocked, snippet only).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Coremark 1.0: ~7% slower than native' (no runtime baseline). Independent, search snippets only (pages blocked): Frank Denis, 'The best WebAssembly runtime may be no runtime at all' (00f.net, 2023-12-11): a test module took 124.76 s user time under Wasmtime vs 73.38 s after w2c2 translation and zig cc compilation (1.70x, derived from the snippet numbers; the snippet does not say the module was the libsodium suite). Andy Wingo, 'wastrel, a profligate implementation of webassembly' (wingolog, 2025-10-30): on CoreMark Wastrel is 2-5% slower than native, w2c2 a further 2-5% slower, and Wasmtime 30-40% slower than GCC (roughly 1.2-1.35x in w2c2's favour, derived from snippet numbers).
compiler_and_flags: examples/coremark/Makefile: CFLAGS += -O3, compiler ($(CC)) unstated; Frank Denis's run compiled the generated C with zig cc (snippet only)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time Wasm to portable C translator (inspired by wabt wasm2c): output must be compiled per module; runs on many OSes and architectures including big-endian; WASI and threads support; no JIT.
caveats: No compiler, CPU or runtime baseline for the README figure; all Wasmtime numbers are from search snippets of blocked posts (00f.net, wingolog.org), and the CoreMark comparison is Andy Wingo's (Wastrel author), not Frank Denis's. Safety is not equivalent to Wasmtime: w2c2_base.h defaults W2C2_RUNTIME_CHECKS to 0, which compiles out memory range checks on every load and store (and atomic alignment checks), and wasmMemoryAllocate takes linear memory from calloc/realloc with no guard pages, so default w2c2 output does not trap on out-of-bounds Wasm memory accesses as a sandboxing runtime does; the opt-in checks only landed on 2026-09-21 (PR #183), so every published comparison ran the unchecked code. The 2026 follow-up post's 0.814x-of-Wasmtime figure is for WABT wasm2c, not w2c2.

name: wisp
baseline: wasmtime Winch (baseline compiler); wasmer Singlepass; wasmtime Cranelift on fib
workload: Whole-process wall time (including startup and compilation) of seven programs (primes, fib, matmul, raytrace, compress, json, regex) compiled to wasm32-wasip1, plus compile-only time for a 1.36 MB regex.wasm; median of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: Compile-only (wall clock, median): regex.wasm (1.36 MB) wisp 16.3 ms vs wasmtime Winch 24.2 ms, wasmer Singlepass 31.5 ms, wasmtime Cranelift 71.6 ms, wasmer Cranelift 82.0 ms; json.wasm (0.19 MB) wisp 4.5 ms vs Winch 8.3, Singlepass 14.2, wasmtime Cranelift 16.0, wasmer Cranelift 28.8. End to end (whole process, seconds): fib 34 wisp 0.022 vs wasmtime Cranelift 0.024, Winch 0.031, wasmer Singlepass 0.028; raytrace 0.054 vs Winch 0.066; json 0.263 vs Winch 0.325; regex 0.308 vs Winch 0.341. Slower than Winch on primes (0.120 vs 0.070), matmul (0.056 vs 0.049) and compress (0.713 vs 0.517), and 1.5-2.5x slower than wasmtime Cranelift on six of seven programs.
compiler_and_flags: wisp: cargo build --release (Cargo.toml release profile with debug = 1; rustc version not recorded for the run, README says developed on 1.98). Guest programs: cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1. Baselines: wasmtime 49.0.1 and wasmer 7.5.0 release binaries run with -C cache=n / --disable-cache, Winch via -C compiler=winch (bench/run.py).
hardware: Apple M5, 10 cores, Darwin 27.0.0 (macOS 27); machine shared with other work while measuring
tradeoffs: Compact (about 12,600 lines of Rust) runtime with validator, register-style interpreter and a single-pass AArch64 baseline compiler (macOS AArch64 only, Linux paths untested); passes 27,416 spec assertions on both engines; explicit bounds checks and no cross-block register allocation.
caveats: The README says plainly that wisp is 1.5-2.5x slower than wasmtime Cranelift end to end on six of seven programs (only fib is faster, 0.022 vs 0.024 s, within noise). It also loses to Winch on primes, compress and matmul. The compile-time comparison is not like for like: wasmtime and wasmer compile functions in parallel and write the artefact to disk, while wisp compiles single-threaded in one process. All timings are whole-process wall clock (start-up included), median of only 5 runs, on a machine shared with other work. Own benchmarks only, 0 stars, 15 commits made 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-02, very new. The compiler runs only on AArch64 macOS (Linux/AArch64 paths are untested and disabled; other hosts use the interpreter, which is 3-8x slower than the compiler). No SIMD, threads or Wasm 3.0 proposals. A Rust library with no C API header yet, so not callable from C++ without bindings.

name: Daslang (daScript)
baseline: Lua 5.5.1 and QuickJS 2026-06-04 (the same table also has LuaJIT 2.1 with -joff, Luau 0.736, Quirrel 4.29.1, Mono --interpreter)
workload: 16 kernels (sha256, dictionary, n-bodies, spectral norm, mandelbrot, exp loop, string2float, particles kinematics, queen, interop host calls, primes loop, tree, sort, fibonacci loop, float2string, fibonacci recursive); each cell is the median of five samples, each sample runs the kernel as often as fits a 0.5 s budget; interpreter lane compared with the Lua and QuickJS interpreters
claimed_speedup: On the Linux Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE interpreted table the DAS interpreter beats Lua and QuickJS on all 16 kernels: sha256 0.002510s vs Lua 0.068548s vs QuickJS 0.021312s; mandelbrot 0.001791s vs 0.056917s vs 0.006346s; sort 0.015450s vs 0.045629s vs 0.037570s; dictionary 0.011193s vs 0.038771s vs 0.047221s; tree 0.023617s vs 0.031137s vs 0.061180s; fibonacci recursive 0.048174s vs 0.048747s vs 0.088087s (about parity with Lua). Same pattern on Apple M1 Max (sha256 0.002792s vs Lua 0.068824s vs QuickJS 0.023714s). Ratios such as 27x vs Lua on sha256 and 8.5x vs QuickJS are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 19.1.7 on Linux, AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 on macOS; daslang 0.6.4 SDK (consumed through find_package(DAS), built separately from the daScript repo), LLVM 22.1.5. dasProfile's CMakeLists.txt forces CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG on Clang; the '-O3' comment in the file refers to the C++ lane). Lua 5.5.1 is compiled from the SHA256-pinned lua.org tarball inside the same Release project (linit.c patched to add a profile_native module); QuickJS 2026-06-04 is built from the pinned bellard.org tarball with its upstream Makefile (hosts/quickjs_host.mk includes it), so QuickJS uses its own default flags.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE w/ Radeon 780M Graphics (Linux) and Apple M1 Max (macOS)
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars (GaijinEntertainment/daScript); 0 stars on the benchmark repo borisbat/dasProfile
tradeoffs: Statically typed language with its own syntax (not drop-in for Lua or JavaScript code); zero-copy C++ interop by design; three execution tiers (interpreter, AOT to C++, LLVM JIT); interpreter startup is slower than Lua/QuickJS (hello world 0.0187s macOS / 0.0261s Linux vs about 0.0024-0.0039s for Lua and QuickJS).
caveats: The benchmark repo is written and maintained by the daslang lead developer (borisbat also merges on the daScript repo), so this is a first-party suite although it is fully public and reproducible; dasProfile shows no licence (no LICENSE file; the language repo is BSD-3-Clause). The daslang SDK's own build flags are set by the daScript repo, not stated in dasProfile. LuaJIT -joff beats the DAS interpreter on 'tree' and 'fibonacci recursive' on Linux, Mono --interpreter beats it on 'tree' on both platforms, and Lua is within about 1% on Linux fibonacci recursive (0.048174s vs 0.048747s); the Linux DAS dictionary cell has ±25% spread. A separate third-party suite (sashi0034/script-language-benchmark, Windows, Visual Studio 17 2022, code generated with Codex and flagged by its author as unreviewed, CPU not stated) reports Daslang fastest on 13 of 16 workloads against Lua and AngelScript (fibonacci_recursive 266.421 vs Lua 599.702) but Lua wins sort (6.175 vs 237.142 ms) and string2float (68.624 vs 107.174 ms); the two suites use different kernel code, so the sort result is not directly comparable with the dasProfile row where DAS wins.

name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen)
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.1 interpreter (also compared against the LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter)
workload: 44 Lua benchmarks in luabench/ (list in run_bench.sh; k-nucleotide and revcomp read a 5,000,000-line FASTA input). The README footnote says 5 repetitions with a geometric mean; the current run_bench.sh runs each benchmark 7 times. Interpreter vs LuaJIT's interpreter (JIT off) and vs PUC Lua 5.1, GC disabled in all implementations.
claimed_speedup: README: interpreter is 34.6% faster than LuaJIT's interpreter and 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter (geometric average over all benchmarks). OOPSLA 2026 paper abstract (WebSearch snippet only): over 44 benchmarks the interpreter is 2.79x faster than PUC Lua and 1.31x faster than LuaJIT's interpreter; the baseline JIT is 4.60x faster than PUC Lua but on average 33% slower than LuaJIT's optimizing JIT (faster on 13 of 44).
compiler_and_flags: Current build: Clang/LLVM 19.1.6 patched and built from source in the repo's docker image (dockerfile/build_docker_image.sh), RELEASE flavor '-DNDEBUG -O3 -fno-pic -fno-pie -mbmi -msse4 -mfsgsbase' (CMakeLists.txt), built via 'python3 ljr-build make release'. run_bench.sh pins to CPU core 4 with taskset and wall-clock-times each benchmark with bash time, sleeping 3 s between runs. The toolchain behind the README numbers and the builds and flags of the LuaJIT and PUC Lua baselines (GC disabled) are not stated.
hardware: Intel i7-12700H laptop, 32GB DDR4, benchmarks pinned with taskset (README footnote)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 semantics only; x86-64 Linux only; garbage collector not implemented; package library (require, module) missing; the Lua table is rebuilt on hidden classes; build needs Docker and a custom LLVM-based generator toolchain; the interpreter is generated from a bytecode semantics description (Deegen) rather than hand-written.

README names no PUC Lua or LuaJIT versions or their build flags. Single laptop; run_bench.sh notes thermal fluctuation of about 10 percent. The JIT tiers are not finished in the repo (README says ongoing; last commit is 2025-02-18), so the JIT numbers exist only in the paper. name: nanobind
baseline: pybind11 (also Boost.Python, Cython, cppyy)
metric: compile-time; binary size (memory); call latency (runtime overhead)
workload: Generated binding microbenchmark: function-heavy module of 720 trivial functions (all permutations of six integer/float argument types) and class-heavy module of 252 small structs with constructor and sum() (the generator stops after i > 250, so not 720); compile time and stripped binary size of each module, and runtime of calling test_0000 10M times and constructing Struct0 + sum() 2.5M times, each in debug (-O0 -g3) and size-optimised (-Os -g0) builds, median of 5 runs.
claimed_speedup: Per-bar labels in the page's SVG plots (ratios relative to nanobind). The page prose says '~2.7-4.4x vs pybind11', but the 4.4x label belongs to Cython's class [opt] column; the pybind11 maximum is 3.1x (4.0x with smart_holder). claimed_speedup: ARM64 dashboard measured 2026-10-04 (Escargot fc608b59b): SunSpider 823.2 ms vs QuickJS 981.6 ms; Octane 2,198 vs 1,689; Web Tooling 1.07 vs 0.89 runs/s. Fixed-work memory average / peak RSS: Octane 85.7 / 157.4 MiB vs QuickJS 161.4 / 226.5; Web Tooling 171.6 / 212.7 vs 375.9 / 546.1; SunSpider 14.2 / 23.6 vs 5.3 / 9.0 (QuickJS lower). name: LuaBridge3
baseline: Sol3 (sol2) and vanilla LuaBridge (C++ Lua binding overhead over the plain Lua C API)
workload: Per-operation binding overhead in nanoseconds across 34 cases (global and table get/set, chained table access, free, member, static and derived method calls, userdata properties, shared-pointer ownership, multi-return, lambda captures, optionals, converters), Google Benchmark, all three libraries on embedded Lua 5.4.8, each case in isolation.
claimed_speedup: README chart Images/benchmarks.png (ns per operation, lower is better, 34 cases): against Sol3, LuaBridge3 is faster on 20 of 30 shared cases (member function call 152.4 vs 356.9, derived method call 91.8 vs 260.5, c function 44.2 vs 116.2, static member function call 88.4 vs 212.1, shared ptr pass 61.7 vs 123.2, userdata property getter 86.4 vs 165.5, userdata variable write 79.7 vs 161.2), slower on 9 (table get 29.1 vs 17.9, table chained get 69.6 vs 28.0, table chained set 56.5 vs 26.8, table global string get 39.7 vs 11.9, table set 18.3 vs 17.2, multi return 49.7 vs 44.8, stateful function object 40.0 vs 37.4, c function through lua in c 40.4 vs 34.3, lua function in c 26.8 vs 25.7) and tied on optional failure (14.3). Against vanilla LuaBridge it is faster on 12 of 22 shared cases (table get 29.1 vs 57.1, optional success 26.8 vs 110.0, table chained get 69.6 vs 156.7) and slower on 10 (c function 44.2 vs 34.3, member function call 152.4 vs 148.7, static member function call 88.4 vs 60.9, lambda capture 45.1 vs 32.8, multi return lua 48.3 vs 33.0, return userdata 167.2 vs 142.0). The headline userdata variable access rows (70.2 vs Sol3 299.9 and vanilla 269.3) are not like-for-like: LuaBridge3's script does one read, the other two do two reads and a write. Win/loss counts derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (Benchmarks/README.md), Google Benchmark v1.8.4, Lua 5.4.8 sources compiled into each executable; Sol3 built with SOL_ALL_SAFETIES_ON=1 and SOL_NO_EXCEPTIONS=1. No LTO flag is set in the CMake files despite the README's link-time-optimization wording; compiler and compiler version not stated.
tradeoffs: Dependency-free binding that works with PUC Lua, LuaJIT, Luau and Ravi; supports many C++17/20/23 std types, lambdas and multiple inheritance; works with or without exceptions.
caveats: First-party chart only, embedded as an image (Images/benchmarks.png); no hardware, compiler or compiler version stated. Harness is not like-for-like: (1) userdata variable access, access large and access last run 'return b.var' for LuaBridge3 but 'b.var = b.var + 1.0 return b.var' (two reads plus a write) for Sol3 and vanilla LuaBridge, so the largest claimed wins (70.2 vs 299.9 ns) compare one operation against three; (2) LuaBridge3 and vanilla cases invoke the Lua script with raw lua_getglobal + lua_pcall while every Sol3 script case goes through sol's lua["name"]() proxy lookup and call each iteration, adding C++-side overhead only to Sol3 (Sol3 c function 116.2 vs c function through lua in c 34.3, a gap of about 82 ns that LuaBridge3 does not show, 44.2 vs 40.4; rough inference derived from page data). On cases that use each library's own C++ API on both sides (table get/set, chained, global get, multi return, stateful function object), Sol3 is mostly faster. Vanilla LuaBridge beats LuaBridge3 on 10 of 22 shared cases, mostly call paths. Sol2 version is ambiguous: Benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt pins v3.3.0 while Benchmarks/README.md says v3.5.0, and vanilla LuaBridge is fetched from master. README says it 'competes directly with sol2', not that it beats it. Baseline (other binding libraries) is not in the category list (Lua, Duktape, QuickJS). Derived from vinniefalco/LuaBridge per README.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua benchmark github' (Lua binding results); README and benchmarks.png fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com

verification.tier_reason: First-party Google Benchmark code is public (Benchmarks/benchmark_luabridge3.cpp, benchmark_sol3.cpp, benchmark_luabridge.cpp; Release build, embedded Lua 5.4.8), but no compiler, flags beyond the CMake build type, or CPU model are stated, so not A; the numbers exist only in the README chart image Images/benchmarks.png.
verification.notes: Numbers in the record match the chart, but the claim is overstated: the biggest wins (userdata variable access 70.2 vs 299.9/269.3 ns) time one property read for LuaBridge3 against a read-modify-write-read for Sol3 and vanilla, and every Sol3 script case pays an extra lua["name"]() proxy call that the LuaBridge3 harness avoids with raw lua_pcall. Keep at C with harness flaws documented; it is slower than vanilla LuaBridge on 10 of 22 shared cases and slower than Sol3 on most C++-side table cases.

name: Luau
baseline: PUC Lua 5.x interpreter (Lua 5.1 to 5.4)
workload: Interpreter dispatch loop, table library, string library and garbage collector sweep, as described in the project's performance guide.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter 'noticeably faster than Lua 5.x (including Lua 5.4 ... doesn't come close)'; table.sort about 4x speedup on average; table insert/remove/move 3x and more vs un-tuned versions; paged GC sweeper 2-3x faster than Lua/LuaJIT linked-list sweep and 16 bytes less per object; table length 50+% faster.
compiler_and_flags: Interpreter tuned for Clang and recent MSVC (per guide); no flags stated
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars; scripting layer of Roblox, also adopted in commercial games per README
tradeoffs: Derived from Lua 5.1 with its own type annotations and a sandboxing model (safeenv via luaL_sandbox) that the fastest paths rely on; API mostly Lua 5.1 compatible with caveats; interpreter-first design, JIT/native codegen is optional and not available everywhere.
caveats: First-party documentation page with ratios but no workload list, hardware, compiler flags or raw numbers, so tier C. The interpreter claim ('noticeably faster than Lua 5.x ... Lua 5.4 ... doesn't come close') has no number; the ~4x table.sort figure names no baseline; table insert/remove/move 3x is 'compared to un-tuned versions'; the 50+% table length gain is versus the default binary search computed from scratch. The repo has bench/ (bench.py with --compare for other VMs, micro_tests, gc) but no checked-in result tables. Several gains (fastcall builtins, imports) require the sandboxed pure global environment and are deoptimized by loadstring/getfenv/setfenv. Independent data point against a different baseline: rochus-keller/Are-we-fast-yet Luau/Results.pdf (14 Are-we-fast-yet benchmarks, i5-8350U, GCC 12.2.0, Luau commit 5836a9c, make config=release, 2025-10-25) gives geomean factors relative to LuaJIT 2.1 JIT of 2.39 for Luau default, 2.31 for -g0 -O2, 1.64 for -O2 --codegen, versus 2.32 for LuaJIT -joff; that is, the Luau interpreter is roughly at LuaJIT interpreter speed (about 3% slower), with no PUC Lua 5.x column.

name: Pallene
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.4 interpreter (the Lua 5.4 bundled with Pallene in 2020); LuaJIT and C in the same post
workload: Independent blog: n-queens counter xdamcnt2 (N up to 12, non-recursive, code in github.com/eklausme/c) and an array-of-records float update loop (N=4000, S=1000), each in Pallene, Lua and C. Paper (snippet only): binarytrees, binsearch, centroid, conway, matmul, queen, sieve and others from the repo benchmarks directory.
claimed_speedup: Klausmeier blog (2020): n-queens Pallene 0.32 s (0.31 s with compiler optimization flags) vs Lua 5.4 3.92 s (about 12x, derived from page data; the post says 13x) and vs LuaJIT 0.58 s (about 1.8x, derived from page data), C -O3 0.2 s; array loop Pallene 0.14 s vs Lua 5.4 0.72 s (about 5x, derived from page data), but LuaJIT 0.07 s is 2x faster than Pallene there. Paper (SBLP 2018 / SCP 2020, search snippets only): around ten times faster than Lua on Sieve and Queens, comparable to LuaJIT; more than three times faster than LuaJIT and the Lua-C API on binary search; LuaJIT substantially faster only on Matmul (NaN-boxing gives 8-byte floats vs 16 bytes in Lua and Pallene).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.3.0 on Arch Linux 5.6.6; the C reference built with -march=native -O3; Pallene and Lua 5.4 build flags not stated (a second Pallene run 'with compiler optimization flags' does not name them)
hardware: AMD FX-8120 eight-core, 3.1 GHz max (blog); paper hardware unknown
tradeoffs: Statically typed, ahead-of-time compiled sister language of Lua (README); output is a C extension module, so a C compiler is needed at build time and the code is loaded through require; it is a companion for hot paths, not a replacement interpreter.
caveats: Independent numbers are from one 2020 blog post on two small programs with a 2020 Pallene (older syntax) and an AMD FX-8120; Pallene and Lua flags unstated. name: sol2
baseline: Other C++ Lua binding libraries (LuaBridge, OOLua, Kaguya, luwra, Selene, SWIG, tolua++ and others); floor is the plain Lua C API
workload: Per-operation overhead of binding layers over the Lua C API (member function call, userdata variable access, table get/set, multi-return and others) measured with nonius in the lua-bindings-shootout repo.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Fastest in the land (see: sol2 bar in graph)'; benchmarks page: sol 'seems to take the cake in most categories for speed'. The page has graphs only, no numeric table.
compiler_and_flags: All libraries compiled against a DLL build of Lua 5.3.3, no link-time optimization (per page); compiler and flags otherwise not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 binding for Lua, LuaJIT and others; heavy template use means long compile times; its fast paths (c_call and disabled type checks) trade safety for speed.
caveats: Evidence is first-party graphs from 2018 (page dated May 17th, 2018) from the author's own lua-bindings-shootout (nonius, Lua 5.3.3 DLL per the docs page; shootout README lists plain C on Lua 5.3.4, sol2 v2.20.0 and sol3 'latest'); no numbers in text and no hardware, compiler or flags stated. Approximate values read off benchmark_results/member function call.png: plain_c about 115 ns, sol3 about 135, oolua about 145, sol2 about 150, luwra about 205, luabridge about 420, old sol about 425, toluapp about 590 (read from the image, not text). Third-party counter-evidence: satoren/lua_binding_benchmark result/result.csv (Intel Core i5-4460, GCC 5.3.1, CMake Release, units not stated, lower is better) puts sol2 v2.5.1 fastest among bindings on global table (338.4) and table chain (561.0, below plain API 596.5), but behind kaguya (1006.9), luacppinterface (1002.0) and the plain API (1086.6) on C++ object member call (sol2 1342.9), behind luwra on C function call (234.7 vs 254.8) and returning a class object (1253.3 vs 1314.4), and behind sol v1 on Lua function call (293.4 vs 330.0). A 2026 first-party chart in the LuaBridge3 README shows Sol3 slower than LuaBridge3 on most script-invoked cases (member function call 356.9 vs 152.4 ns) but faster on C++-side table get/set; that harness is biased against Sol3 (extra lua["name"]() call per iteration, unequal userdata access scripts). Binding-layer overhead, not script execution speed; every binding is slower than the plain Lua C API. Baseline (other binding libraries) is not in the category list (Lua, Duktape, QuickJS). Last commit 2025-03-07, so stale.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language C++ faster than Lua benchmark github' (lua binding benchmarks); sol2 README, benchmarks.rst and shootout PNGs fetched

name: yklua (Yk JIT retrofitted into PUC Lua)
language: C (Lua interpreter) with the Rust Yk JIT
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.5.0 (stock lua.org tarball, the version yklua is based on) built with -flto as an LTO baseline
workload: ykjit/yk-benchmarks nightly ReBench suite: 14 Are-We-Fast-Yet Lua benchmarks, 4 Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs (fannkuchredux, spectralnorm, knucleotide, binarytrees), 3 real-world programs (LuLPeg, HashIds, Heightmap) and the in-house BigLoop; 5 process invocations x 10 in-process iterations each, yklua vs stock Lua 5.5.0.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean execution-time ratio yklua/Lua of 0.513 (about 1.95x faster) over 22 benchmarks in the 2026-10-06 11:14 nightly run (index lists 0.504 to 0.519 for the last 10 runs). Per-benchmark mean iteration times from that run's data file (derived from page data): Mandelbrot(500) 370.2 ms vs 63.4 ms (5.84x), BigLoop 3.90x, spectralnorm 3.30x, Heightmap 3.18x, Sieve 3.01x, NBody 2.88x, fannkuchredux 2.33x, Queens 2.15x, Permute 2.08x, Bounce 1.99x, Towers 1.81x, LuLPeg 1.71x, Richards 1.59x, Json 1.52x, knucleotide 1.47x, List 1.37x, CD 1.36x, HashIds 1.35x, binarytrees 1.33x, Storage 1.23x, DeltaBlue 1.11x, Havlak 1.09x; geomean without the in-house BigLoop loop about 1.89x (derived from page data). Laurence Tratt's 2026 blog post reports 'a geometric mean speedup of a little under 2x' with about 400 lines added and under 50 changed in PUC Lua (snippet only); the Mandelbrot 3.2 s to 0.8 s figure in the original record was not found on any page opened.
compiler_and_flags: Baseline: Lua 5.5.0 stock Makefile (gcc -std=gnu99, -O2 in yklua's copy of the same Makefile) with MYCFLAGS=-flto; yklua: ykllvm (yk's LLVM/clang fork) via yk-config release --cflags --cppflags, -O2, -DUSE_YK -DLUA_USE_JUMPTABLE=0 (ykjit/yk-benchmarks common.sh, ykjit/yklua src/Makefile). gcc version not stated.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7F52 16-Core Processor (host bencher14), Debian kernel 6.12.57, recorded in the rebench results file
license: MIT (PUC-Rio Lua notice in src/lua.h and doc/readme.html); no repository-level LICENSE file covering the Yk additions
tradeoffs: Needs the Yk JIT built separately (README); marked experimental; the README says the test suite is currently failing for non-serialised compilation; tracks upstream PUC Lua instead of being stuck at Lua 5.1 like LuaJIT.
caveats: Experimental (README says so) and not drop-in: building needs the yk toolchain (Rust nightly, ykllvm, yk-config). Means include JIT warm-up iterations; gains are uneven (DeltaBlue 1.11x, Havlak 1.09x, Storage 1.23x) and the 5.84x Mandelbrot and 3.90x BigLoop results are loop-heavy microbenchmarks. Baseline and yklua are built by different compilers (gcc -O2 -flto vs ykllvm clang), and yklua disables Lua's jump-table dispatch. Results come from a rolling nightly snapshot on the gh-pages branch (force-pushed each run), so the cited data file may be replaced. Blog figures (under 2x geomean, about 400 lines added, does not reach LuaJIT's peak performance) are snippet only since tratt.net and infoq.com are blocked. No LICENSE file at the repo root: the Lua core carries PUC-Rio's MIT notice but the Yk-specific changes have no stated licence.

name: Ravi
baseline: Lua 5.3 (the dialect it extends; LuaJIT is named as a different-goal alternative)
workload: Numeric micro-benchmarks in tests/performance (fornum loop tests, mandel1 at 4000, fannkuchen at 11, matmul1 at 1000), each as plain Lua and as Ravi-typed variants, timed under Lua 5.3.2, the Ravi interpreter, Ravi with the LLVM JIT, and LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter and JIT.
claimed_speedup: Ravi with the (now archived) LLVM JIT vs Lua 5.3.2, JIT compile time excluded: fornum_test1 8.94 s vs 0.309 s (about 29x), fornum_test3 52.494 s vs 4.748 s (about 11x), fornum_test2 about 2.1x; untyped Lua code gains only 1.6-2.5x (mandel1.lua 20.324 vs 8.056 s, fannkuchen.lua 46.203 vs 28.422 s, matmul1.lua 26.672 vs 16.83 s); with Ravi type annotations about 13x on mandel (1.571 s), 10x on fannkuchen (4.634 s) and 26x on matmul (1.039 s, array read bounds checks disabled) relative to the untyped Lua 5.3.2 run (ratios derived from page data). Typed Ravi roughly matches LuaJIT 2.1 (1.594, 4.672, 1.078 s) but is far slower than LuaJIT on untyped code. The Ravi interpreter alone is within about 5% of Lua 5.3.2. The 2015 Lua Workshop slides show similar numbers (e.g. matmul(1000) 34.604 s Lua 5.3 vs 1.018 s Ravi LLVM).
compiler_and_flags: Ravi and Lua 5.3.2 compiled with Visual C++ 2015 (flags not stated); LLVM 3.9 JIT backend.
hardware: Windows 10 64-bit; CPU not stated.
tradeoffs: Dialect of Lua with optional type annotations (not a drop-in for LuaJIT-style Lua 5.1 code); JIT backend is MIR, with AOT compilation to shared libraries; Lua 5.4 generational GC backported. Compatible with Lua 5.3 programs.
caveats: All numbers are the author's own, from about 2016 (Lua 5.3.2, LLVM 3.9, Visual C++ 2015, Windows 10) with no CPU or flags given. They measure the LLVM JIT backend, which the README says is archived; the current MIR backend has no published numbers that were found, so today's performance is unverified. JIT compilation time is excluded, the large wins need Ravi type annotations (untyped Lua code gains only 1.6-2.5x), and matmul ran with array read bounds checks disabled. name: Chez Scheme
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 3 and Node.js (V8)
workload: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b and mandel.b); plb2 nqueen and matmul.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), Chez Scheme 10.0.0, brainfuck bench.b: 1.758 s vs Node.js 2.954 s, Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s (about 1.68x, 3.23x and 5.35x, derived from page data); Java 1.191 s is faster. mandel.b: 30.884 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s (about 1.03x, 1.12x and 1.33x, derived from page data); Java 13.041 s is faster. Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Chez 9.5.8, Apple M1): nqueen 3.54 s vs luajit 5.31 s, PyPy 6.91 s, Node 3.73 s and Java 3.92 s (faster than all four), but matmul 18.98 s vs luajit 2.66 s, Node 2.88 s, PyPy 4.89 s and Java 1.14 s (7.1x slower than LuaJIT and 16.6x slower than Java, derived from page data); plb2 has no Chez sudoku or bedcov.
compiler_and_flags: kostya: `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program` (common/commands.mk SCHEME_RUN), Chez Scheme 10.0.0 from the Debian chezscheme package; baselines luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23, Node.js v26.5.0, Java 24.0.2, all run with default flags. plb2: src/scheme/run.sh uses the same `scheme --optimize-level 3 --program`, Chez 9.5.8.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (kostya/benchmarks); Apple M1 (plb2)
tradeoffs: Incremental native-code compiler with a Scheme runtime, not a general-purpose embeddable JIT; C interface exists; optimize-level 3 removes safety checks.
caveats: Mixed results: Chez wins only the brainfuck interpreter tests in kostya (the only kostya tests that have a Chez row) and plb2 nqueen; plb2 matmul is 7-17x slower than every JIT baseline (its source stores doubles in a generic Scheme vector, so every element is a boxed flonum). The mandel.b margin over LuaJIT is about 3%. Java (HotSpot) beats Chez on both kostya brainfuck tests. optimize-level 3 is Chez's unsafe mode (type and bounds checks removed), which the baselines do not get. Chez is not a tracing or profiling JIT: the full compiler (Debian chezscheme package) compiles the program to native code when it is loaded, so the category fit is load-time compilation. The brainfuck programs differ in shape across languages (Chez walks a parsed op list recursively; LuaJIT's bf_jit.lua dispatches through one closure per op; Node, Java and C# use a parsed op tree with a switch), so the comparison is per idiomatic implementation, not identical code. plb2 numbers are from Chez 9.5.8 (early 2024 versions) and its author notes his non-C implementations may be suboptimal.

name: FakeLua
baseline: PUC Lua 5.4.7 (LuaJIT not compared)
workload: 51 Lua micro-scenarios in 6 categories (algorithms, strings, tables, function calls, ...), Google Benchmark harness bench_mark, FakeLua JIT_GCC and JIT_TCC backends versus Lua 5.4 and hand-written C++.
claimed_speedup: JIT_GCC vs PUC Lua 5.4 (CPU-time ratios, 2026-08-14 run): Fibonacci n=32 36.6x (277.9 ms vs 7.59 ms CPU), Sum n=5M 30.4x, Popcount n=100K 37.3x, FloatPoly n=1M 34.9x, Recursion n=25 42.9x, TailRecursion n=5K 107.5x (that bench has since been removed from the harness); TCC backend Fibonacci n=32 11.2x (derived from page data: 277.9 ms vs 24.86 ms CPU). Most table and string rows are only 1.0-6.1x (TableChurn 9.3x); GCD 0.45x, ToNumber 0.53x, Variadic 0.91x and StringFind 0.85x are slower, and the Boost.Regex rows are much slower (0.06-0.21x).
compiler_and_flags: Release build, -O3 -DNDEBUG (plus -g3 -fPIC from the top-level CMakeLists); GCC 15.1.0 for the JIT_GCC run, whose generated C is compiled at -O3 at script load; GCC 16.2.0 for the interpreter run. Lua baseline is the system liblua5.4 found via pkg-config (distro build flags not stated); Lua 5.4.7 is named only for the 2026-09-16 interpreter run. Google Benchmark v1.9.4.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7K62 48-Core Processor, 2-vCPU VM at 2595 MHz, load average 5.87 during the run (GCC/TCC JIT run, 2026-08-14); AMD EPYC 7551, 16-vCPU KVM (interpreter run, 2026-09-16)
tradeoffs: Runs a Lua 5.4 subset: no coroutines, metatables or require, and no implicit string-number coercion; arena allocation with per-frame reset instead of GC. JIT_GCC shells out to the system GCC at run time (compile latency and a compiler dependency); JIT_TCC uses embedded TinyCC; JIT_INTERP bytecode VM needs no compiler.
caveats: Baseline is PUC Lua 5.4 (distro liblua5.4), not LuaJIT, so the result does not show a win over LuaJIT. Lua source is compiled to C and built by GCC/TCC at script load; that compile time is outside the timed region. The GCC JIT numbers come from a 2026-08-14 run on a loaded 2-vCPU cloud VM (wall times about 1.6x CPU times; the ratios use CPU time) and predate many later correctness fixes, including math-specialization eligibility fixes (commits 236a757 and 598632f, 2026-10-02); those fixes target shadowed, nested, multi-return and vararg functions that the bench scripts do not use, and the harness verifies every result, but the GCC run has not been repeated on current code. The TailRecursion bench (107.5x) was removed from the harness on 2026-09-18 (commit 12fbcd7), so that row is not reproducible from HEAD. The regex rows used Boost.Regex; commit a55a4bf (2026-10-03) implements Lua 5.4 patterns, so those rows may be obsolete. Some StringFindPattern/StringGmatch raw lines predate a workload correction (the page says so). The hand-written C++ reference column is not credible: the page says some references are folded, and C++ Sum n=5M took 27.4 ms CPU against 1.55 ms for FakeLua's GCC-compiled version of the same loop, so 'faster than C++' claims should be ignored. The bytecode interpreter tier is 1.3x to 7.6x slower than Lua 5.4 in its algorithm rows (34x on TailRecursion). Very young, fast-moving repository.

name: Julia
language: Julia (C/C++ runtime on LLVM; embeddable from C/C++ through libjulia)
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1, PyPy 3 (7.3.x), Node.js (V8) and OpenJDK HotSpot, on the same CPU-bound algorithms
workload: Single-threaded CPU-bound programs written with the same algorithm in every language: kostya/benchmarks brainfuck interpreter (bench.b, mandel.b) and naive matrix multiply; plb2 nqueen, matmul (1500x1500), sudoku, bedcov.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks), brainfuck bench.b: Julia 1.564 s vs Lua/luajit 5.686 s, Python/pypy 9.398 s, Node.js 2.954 s (about 3.6x, 6.0x and 1.9x, derived from page data); Java 1.191 s is faster. mandel.b: Julia 30.315 s vs luajit 31.804 s, Node.js 34.692 s, pypy 41.153 s; Java 13.041 s is faster. matmul 'Julia (no BLAS)': 1.113 s vs Java 3.057 s, Node.js 3.212 s, pypy 3.263 s (about 2.7x vs OpenJDK, derived from page data). Second source plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2, Apple M1): Julia 1.10.0 nqueen 3.02 s, matmul 0.76 s, sudoku 2.18 s, bedcov 1.96 s vs luajit 5.31/2.66/4.48/10.52 s, PyPy 7.3.14 6.91/4.89/8.82/6.27 s, Java 20.0.1 3.92/1.14/3.20/3.04 s, Node 21.5.0 3.73/2.88/3.77/2.45 s (faster than all four on all four tasks).
compiler_and_flags: kostya/benchmarks: julia v1.11.6 run as `julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no`; Java 24.0.2, Node.js v26.5.0, luajit 2.1.1748495995, pypy 7.3.23 (Python 3.11.15), Docker on Debian; run commands in common/commands.mk. plb2 versions in its README table (Julia 1.10.0, Java 20.0.1, PyPy 7.3.14, LuaJIT 2.1, Node 21.5.0).
hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel Xeon E-2324G; plb2: Apple M1 MacBook Pro
tradeoffs: Per-process JIT warmup and large footprint (kostya bench.b base RSS about 244 MB vs 2.5 MB for LuaJIT); package precompilation latency; garbage collected; embedding in C++ goes through the libjulia C API and is heavier than embedding LuaJIT.
caveats: Workload specific: Java beats Julia on kostya's bench.b and mandel.b, and in kostya's other tests Julia loses to most baselines: base64 3.085 s vs Node.js 0.635 s and Java 1.435 s (Julia does beat PyPy 3.534 s there); primes 0.680 s vs Java 0.161 s, Node.js 0.207 s, luajit 0.309 s and PyPy 0.617 s; JSON (JSON3) 0.700 s vs Node.js 0.374 s, Java DSL-JSON 0.571 s and PyPy 0.606 s. In plb2 Julia beats all four baselines. The kostya run uses --check-bounds=no (bounds checks removed) and plb2's Julia sources use @inbounds in hot loops, which other languages' sources do not. The kostya 'no BLAS' matmul source is not a plain triple loop: it uses @simd ivdep and @fastmath (allowing reassociation and vectorized FMA, which Java and V8 cannot do) and wraps the outer loop in Threads.@threads (single-threaded here, since JULIA_RUN passes no -t and sets no JULIA_NUM_THREADS). Julia matmul rows at 0.12-0.17 s use BLAS and are not comparable. The kostya brainfuck bf.jl scans raw characters and brackets at run time, while the Node, Java and C# versions parse an op tree first, so the code shapes differ. Each program runs a small verify() before the timer starts, which warms the JIT on the same functions, so most compile time is outside the timed region; plb2 includes startup and compile time. kostya's docker/Dockerfile now pins julia-1.12.6 while the README environment lists v1.11.6, so the published numbers predate the current image.

name: Graal.js (GraalJS)
baseline: Node.js (V8)
workload: Are We Fast Yet suite (CD, DeltaBlue, Havlak, Json, Richards, Bounce, List, Mandelbrot, NBody, Permute, Queens, Sieve, Storage, Towers) after warmup, peak performance, runtime normalised to Java 1.8.0_91.

Per benchmark Graal.js is faster on 8 of 14 (Bounce 1.26 vs 12.25, CD, DeltaBlue, List, NBody, Richards, Storage, Towers), slower on 5 (Havlak 12.22 vs 10.24, Json 1.60 vs 1.14, Mandelbrot, Permute 3.06 vs 2.13, Queens) and tied on Sieve (3.61). Excluding the Bounce outlier the geomeans are 2.33 vs 2.58, about 1.11x (derived from page data). Counter-evidence: kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, https://github.com/kostya/jit-benchmarks) has Graal.js 22.3.1 (graalnode, node 16.18.1), native and JVM modes, slower than Node.js 19.7.0 on all 13 benchmarks (e.g. brainfuck 76.16 s native / 52.08 s JVM vs 5.88 s, nbody 4.82 / 5.59 vs 0.82, regexdna 10.0 / 6.68 vs 1.06, matmul 0.51 / 0.30 vs 0.26).

tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM (Java and Truffle/Graal compiler); long warmup and high memory; native-image distribution exists; Java interoperability; JavaScript only, no V8 embedding API from C++.
caveats: The only measured win is from June 2016 (early Graal.js vs Node.js 6.2), and its geomean edge is driven by Bounce, where Node.js was 12.25x Java; without Bounce the gap is about 1.11x. Node.js is still faster on 5 of 14 AWFY benchmarks (Graal.js has the better median, 2.13 vs 2.54). The independent, reproducible kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023) shows Graal.js 22.3.1 slower than Node.js 19.7.0 on all 13 benchmarks, often by 2x to 13x, so current Graal.js should not be presented as faster than V8. name: TPDE (TPDE-LLVM back-end)
baseline: LLVM -O0 code generation (clang/llc back-end)
workload: Compiling LLVM-IR to machine code at -O0 quality with TPDE-LLVM versus LLVM's -O0 back-end.
claimed_speedup: README: TPDE-LLVM compiles 10--20x faster than LLVM -O0 with similar code quality. docs/tpde-llvm/main.md: compile times typically 10--20x faster than the LLVM -O0 back-end with similar execution time; code size ~10-30% larger for -O0 IR and similar for -O1 IR.
stars_or_usage: 671 stars; used for a Wasmtime back-end and in Umbra per search snippets
tradeoffs: Single-pass back-end aimed at -O0 quality baseline code, not optimized code. Targets ELF-based x86-64 and AArch64 (Armv8.1) only. Usable as library for JIT, as tpde-llc tool, or in Clang/Flang 22+ with a patch. Needs LLVM-IR (or another SSA IR through its adapters).
caveats: Compile-time win only; generated code is -O0 quality, not comparable to V8 TurboFan, HotSpot C2 or LLVM -O2. TPDE-LLVM supports a subset of LLVM-IR (x86-64-v1 and AArch64 Armv8.1 ELF only; Clang -O2 and higher IR typically fails on unsupported vector operations and falls back to the full LLVM back-end); code size 10-30% larger for -O0 IR. The README cites only the arXiv preprint 2505.22610; the peer-reviewed version is CGO 2026 (Schwarz, Kamm, Engelke) with an artifact on Zenodo (record 17619677) running SPEC CPU 2017, which is proprietary, so the evaluation is not fully reproducible. Paper numbers are snippet only and differ by version: arXiv snippet says 8-24x faster than LLVM -O0 on SPEC CPU 2017 with geomean 12.15x (x86-64) and 18.96x (AArch64) and run time within +-9%; the CGO snippet says 8-26x, geomean 16.2x/18.7x over -O0 and 85.8x/80.0x over -O1. The search agent's Wasmtime/Cranelift figures (4.27x faster compile than Cranelift, Cranelift code 1.64x faster) were not re-checked.
found_via: WebSearch: 'TPDE fast compiler back-end framework compile time faster than LLVM -O0 paper github' and 'TPDE compile time SPECint 2017 LLVM -O0 speedup Cranelift Wasmtime backend CPU evaluation results'
WebSearch: 'copy-and-patch JIT github C++ benchmark faster than LLVM baseline compiler' surfaced the paper; WebSearch for TPDE details, then opened the github.com repo page and README.

verification.tier_reason: The README and docs/tpde-llvm/main.md state the 10-20x compile-time win over the LLVM -O0 back-end (first-party, no methodology), and the evaluation is in a peer-reviewed CGO 2026 paper with a Zenodo artifact (SPEC CPU 2017, x86-64 and AArch64 images); the paper, artifact and CGO page were seen only through search snippets (arxiv.org, home.cit.tum.de, 2026.cgo.org, discourse.llvm.org blocked), and SPEC is proprietary with hardware and flags unseen, so not A.
verification.notes: Record accurate; README and docs carry the 10-20x figure, paper only via snippets (blocked hosts), so B rests on the CGO 2026 acceptance and Zenodo artifact seen in search results. Shortcomings: -O0 code quality only, LLVM-IR subset with fallback, SPEC-based evaluation not reproducible, paper not opened. Candidate for a paper-access retier check (arXiv 2505.22610 or home.cit.tum.de/~engelke/pubs/2602-cgo1.pdf).

name: WasmNow (copy-and-patch WebAssembly baseline compiler)
baseline: Google Chrome (V8) Liftoff baseline WebAssembly compiler; also Wasmer Singlepass named in README
workload: Coremark and PolyBenchC compiled to WebAssembly: compile time and generated-code speed versus Liftoff.
claimed_speedup: Versus Chrome's Liftoff: on Coremark compiles 5x faster while generating 39% faster code; on PolyBenchC compiles 6.5x faster while generating 63% faster code (README).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 10.0.0 (LLVM 10.0.0 release binaries installed in dockerfile/Dockerfile on Ubuntu 18.04); production flavor adds -O3 -DNDEBUG, plus -pthread -mavx2 (CMakeLists.txt); built via pochivm-build cmake/make production. Liftoff/Chrome version and flags not stated in the repo.
tradeoffs: Research-grade proof of concept: README warns not to run untrusted WebAssembly with it. Only WebAssembly 1.0 core, partial WASI, Linux plus docker only, dead code left over from PochiVM. Only a baseline tier; no optimizing tier.
caveats: Peer-reviewed support is the OOPSLA 2021 paper 'Copy-and-Patch Compilation' (Xu and Kjolstad, Distinguished Paper Award); its abstract per search snippet gives 4.9x-6.5x faster compilation and 39%-63% faster generated code than Liftoff on Coremark and PolyBenchC, matching the README; the PDF was not opened (fredrikbk.com, sillycross.github.io, arXiv blocked; no copy in the sillycross.github.io repo). The repo benchmark harness (test_parser.cpp) measures WasmNow only; Liftoff measurements and the CPU model are not in the repo. Beats Liftoff, a baseline tier, not V8's optimizing TurboFan. Research prototype: 4 commits, last in Oct 2021; WebAssembly 1.0 core only with partial WASI (runs Coremark and PolyBenchC, other modules may hit unimplemented imports); requires AVX2 (-mavx2); the author warns not to run untrusted WebAssembly with it (unaudited JIT, sandbox-escape risk).
