name: AsmJit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter AsmJit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md), JIT compilation overhead from EXPLAIN JSON: SUM_int llvmjit 22.263 ms vs asmjit 0.109 ms; GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 45.5 ms vs asmjit 0.245 ms (about 200x less compile time, derived from page data). Query time with JIT forced on: SUM_int llvmjit 68.090 ms vs asmjit 42.201 ms (interpreter 44.859 ms); GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 149.033 ms vs asmjit 98.079 ms (interpreter 117.367 ms). pg_jitter README: AsmJit compile 'hundreds of microseconds' vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; its 'up to 32% faster' for AsmJit on wide-row/deform-heavy queries is relative to the PostgreSQL interpreter, not to LLVM.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Assembler-level C++ API for x86, x86-64, AArch32 and AArch64 with a register allocator in the Compiler layer; no mid-level optimizer; the pg_jitter AsmJit backend supports only arm64 and x86_64.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the numbers measure pg_jitter's AsmJit backend (pg_jitter's own code generator design, no optimization passes) inside PostgreSQL, not AsmJit as a library, and the AsmJit repo carries no benchmark against LLVM. The harness forces jit_above_cost, jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost to 0, so LLVM pays full optimization and inlining on every query and its compile time is inside the measured execution time; execution-only, SUM_int is about 45.8 ms llvmjit vs 42.1 ms asmjit (derived from page data). On the same page the sljit backend compiles about 2x faster than AsmJit (SUM_int 0.052 ms vs 0.109 ms), so AsmJit is not the fastest emitter there. One machine (Apple M1 Pro, macOS), ARM64 only (x86_64 marked TBD), compiler and flags not stated, dated 2026-03-24. Baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not a listed baseline.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'asmjit benchmark code generation speed compared LLVM xbyak sljit JIT assembler performance' surfaced pg_jitter, which uses AsmJit as a backend

verification.tier_reason: Only evidence is pg_jitter's own benchmark page (bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md, harness tests/bench_all_backends.sh) timing pg_jitter's AsmJit backend against PostgreSQL's llvmjit on an Apple M1 Pro; compiler and build flags are not stated and the AsmJit repo has no LLVM comparison of its own, so this indirect first-party-style measurement stays at C.
verification.notes: Numbers on the record match the pg_jitter PG18 page; I added the page's compile-time table since the metric is compile-time, and fixed the 'up to 32%' claim, which is against the interpreter. Metadata checked: Zlib, 4.6k stars, 597 forks, last commit 2026-09-22, active. Shortcomings: indirect evidence via a third-party PostgreSQL extension, LLVM forced to full optimization on every query, sljit beats AsmJit on compile time on the same page, ARM64-only single machine.

name: CPython copy-and-patch JIT
baseline: CPython standard interpreter (tail-calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS), built with all optimizations
workload: pyperformance 1.14.0 suite run by bench_runner (13 benchmarks excluded from the geomean, including unpack_sequence, pickle and asyncio_tcp), JIT-enabled build versus the same CPython commit (main, 3.16.0a0, 80f9aa0, 2026-09-25) built without the JIT.
claimed_speedup: Python 3.15 What's New (Doc/whatsnew/3.15.rst): 7-8% geometric mean pyperformance improvement for the JIT over the standard interpreter built with all optimizations on x86-64 Linux; 11-12% over the tail-calling interpreter on AArch64 macOS; per-benchmark JIT vs no-JIT from roughly 15% slowdown to over 100% speedup, ignoring unpack_sequence. Linked raw run (pyperf_bench, commit 80f9aa0, 2026-09-25): x86-64 overall geometric mean 1.079x faster (vs-base.md). From the run's pyperf JSONs (derived from page data, 105 benchmarks after bench_runner exclusions): x86-64 geomean 1.075x, per benchmark 0.89x (k_core) to 2.47x (richards_super); macOS arm64 JIT+tail-call vs tail-call geomean 1.113x, 0.82x (k_core) to 2.23x (richards); the excluded unpack_sequence runs 0.56x (x86-64) and 0.71x (macOS), i.e. slower with the JIT.
compiler_and_flags: x86-64 Linux run: GCC 13.3.0, CFLAGS -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-omit-frame-pointer -mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer, configure --enable-optimizations --with-lto=full (PGO+LTO) with and without --enable-experimental-jit=yes. macOS arm64 run: Clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101), same configure flags plus --with-tail-call-interp on both sides. JIT stencils are generated at build time with LLVM 21 (Tools/jit/README.md). Flags from pyperf JSON metadata in savannahostrowski/pyperf_bench.
hardware: x86-64: Intel Core i5-8400 @ 2.80GHz (6 cores, intel_pstate no turbo, performance governor), Linux 6.8.0, glibc 2.39 (runner 'ripley'). AArch64: Apple Silicon Mac on macOS 26.5.2 (runner 'jones'; CPU model not recorded in metadata).
tradeoffs: Experimental, off by default; enabled at build time with --enable-experimental-jit and at run time with PYTHON_JIT. Needs LLVM only at build time. Per the 3.14 notes it is not recommended for production and free-threaded builds do not support it. Machine-code unwinding support added in 3.15.
caveats: Compares the JIT with CPython's own interpreter, not with PyPy, LuaJIT, V8 or HotSpot, so it does not beat the jits category baselines; the gain is small (7-12% geomean) and some benchmarks slow down (k_core 11-18% slower; unpack_sequence, excluded from the geomean, about 1.4-1.8x slower, derived from the run's JSON). name: Eclipse OpenJ9
baseline: HotSpot (AdoptOpenJDK 11.0.7)

claimed_speedup: DayTrader 3 on OpenJDK 9: with AOT enabled (shared class cache populated by an earlier cold run) OpenJ9 startup is almost 40% lower than HotSpot, with AOT plus -Xquickstart almost 50% lower (page headline '2x faster startup'); with no options OpenJ9 starts slightly slower than HotSpot. Footprint about 60% less right after startup; during ramp-up HotSpot used about 80% more RSS (headline '40% less footprint'). Similar peak throughput, reached about 7 minutes sooner by OpenJ9. Single-core cloud test (AOT plus -Xtune:virtualized): headline '4x faster ramp up', HotSpot needs about 30 minutes to peak vs 7.5 minutes for default OpenJ9. Newer pages in the same repo: OpenJDK 11 DayTrader7 51-55% faster startup and 45-57% smaller startup footprint with SCC/AOT (benchmark/openjdk11-daytrader7.md); Quarkus REST+CRUD 64-66% faster startup, 18-37% smaller startup footprint (benchmark/quarkus.md).

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT (JIT mode); README also compares against wasmtime, wasm3 and Luau
workload: Embedded scripting micro-benchmarks run in the sandbox as RISC-V guest code with binary translation, versus the same tasks as LuaJIT scripts: host-to-guest call overhead, syscall cost, integer math loops, sieve of 10M.
claimed_speedup: Gist, libriscv with libtcc binary translation vs LuaJIT, medians over 200x1200 samples with call overhead subtracted for both: call overhead 2 vs 156 ns; call args=8 7 vs 197 ns; syscall args=0 10 vs 174 ns; syscall string 13 vs 186 ns; complex syscall 50 vs 873 ns; integer math 6 vs 52 ns; array append 5 vs table append 18 ns; memcpy 18 vs 87 ns; memset 15 vs 67 ns; micro threads 102 vs coroutines 166 ns; sieve(10M) 80 vs 123 ms; fib(40) 66 vs 66 ns (equal); taylor(1K) 2234 vs 858 ns (LuaJIT about 2.6x faster, derived from page data). README: VM function call 3 ns vs ~50-150 ns for other solutions; libriscv can call a 3x-sinf function 5.25-7.25 times before wasmtime has called it once.
hardware: Gist does not state the CPU; the README names a Ryzen 7950X for its other charts (CoreMark 38223 vs 41382 native, about 92%).
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; same organisation maintains godot-sandbox (487 stars)
tradeoffs: Emulator and sandbox for precompiled RISC-V programs rather than a general JIT for a dynamic language; full binary translation needs a C compiler (GCC or TCC) at run time, or the generated C99 can be embedded ahead of time for platforms that forbid executable memory. Needs a RISC-V toolchain to build guest code.
caveats: Gist does not state CPU, compiler flags, LuaJIT version or date (gist last active Oct 2025) and links no harness, so first-party tier C. The wins are mostly host-to-script call and syscall latency, which the author's rvscript README describes as the overhead of calling into Lua/LuaJIT from a game engine; it compares native-compiled RISC-V guest code against Lua scripts, not the same program. LuaJIT is about 2.6x faster on taylor(1K) (858 vs 2234 ns) and equal on fib(40); only sieve(10M) is a classic compute benchmark won (80 vs 123 ms). Benchmarks are hand-picked for game scripting; call overhead is subtracted from every result for both sides. Binary translation needs libtcc or an ahead-of-time translated build; the interpreted libriscv vs LuaJIT comparison is a separate gist. A sandbox/emulator with a JIT-like translator, not a drop-in replacement for LuaJIT as a language implementation.

name: pg_jitter
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit); also PostgreSQL's expression interpreter
workload: PostgreSQL 18.1 queries on 1M-row tables (aggregation, joins, wide rows, text, numeric, jsonb), JIT thresholds set to 0, median of 3 timed runs after 2 warmups, parallel workers off.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md): query time with JIT forced on, SUM_int no JIT 44.859 ms, llvmjit 68.090 ms, sljit 42.401 ms, asmjit 42.201 ms, mir 45.620 ms; GroupBy_5agg no JIT 117.367 ms, llvmjit 149.033 ms, sljit 99.530 ms, asmjit 98.079 ms, mir 125.102 ms. JIT compilation overhead (EXPLAIN JSON): SUM_int llvmjit 22.263 ms vs sljit 0.052 ms, asmjit 0.109 ms, mir 0.345 ms; GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 45.5 ms vs sljit 0.069 ms, asmjit 0.245 ms, mir 1.087 ms. README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): compile time 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' (sljit) and 'hundreds of microseconds' (AsmJit) vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'; sljit '5-25% faster than the interpreter'; average speedup over the interpreter TPC-C 8%, TPC-H 6%, ecommerce 14%, OLAP 42%, CRM ~400%.
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; pg_jitter CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release; compiler, compiler version and PostgreSQL build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: PostgreSQL extension only; beta quality by its own README; jit_above_cost must be lowered from 100000 to about 200-2000; avoid for point lookups; AsmJit backend only on arm64 and x86_64; adds embedded JIT libraries (sljit, AsmJit, MIR) in place of LLVM.
caveats: First-party benchmarks, one machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results marked TBD), dated 2026-03-24 for release 0.3.0. The harness (tests/bench_all_backends.sh) sets jit_above_cost, jit_inline_above_cost and jit_optimize_above_cost to 0, so LLVM runs full optimization and inlining on every query and that compile time is inside the EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution time; most of the win over llvmjit is compile time (execution-only SUM_int about 45.8 ms llvmjit vs 42.3 ms sljit, derived from page data). Default thresholds would keep LLVM off these queries entirely. Per-query gains over the interpreter are small and some queries are slower (COUNT_star 0.94x for all three backends); pg_jitter.deform_cache (on by default) can reuse compiled deform code across the warmup and timed runs in one connection while LLVM recompiles, which may favour pg_jitter (not checked). The CRM benchmark is synthetic and built to show the strongest cases. Requires the author's patched forks of sljit and MIR. README calls the code beta quality. Baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines.

name: sljit
baseline: PostgreSQL LLVM JIT (llvmjit) in the pg_jitter shootout
workload: Machine-code generation for PostgreSQL expression evaluation through the pg_jitter sljit backend (PostgreSQL 18.1, 1M-row tables, thresholds forced to 0).
claimed_speedup: pg_jitter benchmark page (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter/blob/master/bench/ARM64/0.3.0/BENCHMARKS_v18.md), JIT compilation overhead table: SUM_int llvmjit 22.263 ms vs sljit 0.052 ms, GroupBy_5agg 45.5 ms vs 0.069 ms, Wide1K_groupby 2043.286 ms vs 0.071 ms (about 220x to 29,000x less compile time across 106 queries, median about 480x, derived from page data). End-to-end query time with thresholds forced to 0: SUM_int llvmjit 68.090 ms vs sljit 42.401 ms (interpreter 44.859 ms); GroupBy_5agg llvmjit 149.033 ms vs sljit 99.530 ms (interpreter 117.367 ms); sljit beats llvmjit's total time on 106 of 108 queries (derived from page data). README (https://github.com/vladich/pg_jitter): sljit compile 'tens to low hundreds of microseconds' vs LLVM 'tens to hundreds of milliseconds'. The README's 'sljit is the most consistent: 5-25% faster than the interpreter across all workloads' is not borne out by this page: sljit is slower than the interpreter on 27 of 108 queries (down to 0.81x on LIKE_3wild), median 1.11x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: PostgreSQL 18.1; C/C++ compiler and build flags for pg_jitter, sljit and PostgreSQL not stated on the page. Benchmark script: tests/bench_comprehensive.sh in vladich/pg_jitter.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, 32 GB RAM, Darwin 25.2.0 arm64
tradeoffs: Low-level stack-less JIT with a platform-independent API (x86, ARM, RISC-V, s390x, PowerPC, LoongArch, MIPS); you write the code generator yourself (no optimizer); used by PCRE2.
caveats: Indirect evidence: the numbers measure pg_jitter's sljit backend (pg_jitter's own code generator emitting through sljit), not the sljit library alone, and the sljit repo carries no benchmark of its own. pg_jitter's README tells users to build the patched fork vladich/sljit ('bug fixes, extra SIMD opcodes, memory management improvements'), so the measured code may not be upstream zherczeg/sljit. The harness runs llvmjit with jit_inline_above_cost=0 and jit_optimize_above_cost=0 (full LLVM inlining and optimization on every query) while the pg_jitter backends get 500000, which maximizes LLVM's compile time; PostgreSQL's defaults would skip LLVM optimization on cheap queries. With all thresholds at 0, LLVM compile cost dominates the end-to-end totals. Some LIKE/regex wins come from PCRE2 and StringZilla, not sljit codegen. Single machine, ARM64 only (x86_64 results 'TBD'), median of 3 runs, first-party pg_jitter numbers. The baseline is PostgreSQL's LLVM JIT, not one of the category baselines (PyPy, LuaJIT, V8, HotSpot).

name: WARP WebAssembly compiler and runtime (wasm-ecosystem/wasm-compiler)
baseline: V8 Liftoff and V8 TurboFan; SpiderMonkey Baseline and Ion
workload: Normalized compilation speed and execution speed of WebAssembly modules from the open-wasm-compiler-benchmark repo (github.com/Schleifner/open-wasm-compiler-benchmark, which returns 404 as of 2026-10-06, so the inputs are not public), WARP's vb_bench versus V8 d8 (Liftoff, TurboFan) and SpiderMonkey js shell (Baseline, Ion) and native clang builds, timed by scripts/benchmark/run_bench.py.
claimed_speedup: README quadrant chart (normalized scores, compilation / execution): WARP 0.8316 / 0.8172; V8 Liftoff 0.747 / 0.4275; V8 TurboFan 0.0423 / 0.8505; SpiderMonkey Baseline 0.8136 / 0.3456; SpiderMonkey Ion 0.099 / 0.8163; native clang 0.5 (comp. speed N/A) / 0.873.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark guide (scripts/benchmark/Readme.md): vb_bench built with clang/clang++, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, -DINTERRUPTION_REQUEST=0 -DEAGER_ALLOCATION=1, VB_ENABLE_DEV_FEATURE=OFF; V8 d8 built with tools/dev/gm.py x64.release and run with --no-wasm-lazy-compilation --liftoff or --no-liftoff --single-threaded; SpiderMonkey built with an optimized mozconfig and run with --wasm-compiler=baseline or ion --cpu-count=1. Compiler, V8 and SpiderMonkey versions not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler and runtime aimed at embedded systems (x86_64, aarch64, tricore; aarch32 not implemented), written in C++14 with no external dependencies in production code; 187 kB stripped binary (AArch64, Clang 17, macOS). Compiles ahead of time into an ELF-like artifact that the runtime instantiates.
caveats: Result is a normalized unitless quadrant chart; run_bench.py prints wall-clock means and a score of 10000/geomean, but how the 0-1 chart values were derived is not documented, and native clang's compile score is a placeholder 0.5 ('comp. speed N/A'). CPU model and tool versions are not stated. Benchmark inputs (Schleifner/open-wasm-compiler-benchmark) are not publicly reachable (404). Harness flaws: the compilation benchmark times the whole process with /usr/bin/time -p (10 ms resolution), so d8 and SpiderMonkey js-shell startup and JS harness load are charged to their compile time while WARP runs as a small native binary, which favours WARP; default is a single run per module (-n 1); the 'V8 Liftoff' runs do not pass --no-wasm-tier-up, so hot code may tier up to TurboFan. WARP's execution score (0.8172) is below V8 TurboFan (0.8505) and native clang (0.873) and about equal to SpiderMonkey Ion (0.8163); its win is compile speed at near-optimizing-tier execution speed, and clearly over the single-pass baselines Liftoff (0.4275) and SpiderMonkey Baseline (0.3456). Backing paper (Scheidl, Valent-Blocks, iCCECE 2020) was not opened (IEEE and ResearchGate blocked); a search snippet only says WebAssembly overhead on embedded targets fell from 87% to 21%.

name: TruffleRuby
baseline: CRuby 4.0.6 (MRI interpreter), also CRuby with --jit (YJIT)
workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck bench.b, matmul, primes, JSON, base64, run as the same Ruby scripts under each Ruby implementation.
claimed_speedup: Are We Fast Yet (https://github.com/smarr/are-we-fast-yet/blob/master/docs/performance.md, 2016-06-20, peak performance, runtime factor over Java 1.8.0_91) 'JRuby+Truffle' (the former name of TruffleRuby): geomean 2.36 (sd 0.94, median 2.64, max 4.31) vs Node.js 2.89 (sd 3.33, median 2.54, max 12.25), about 1.22x lower geomean (derived from page data). It is faster than Node.js on only 6 of 14 benchmarks (Bounce 1.41 vs 12.25, DeltaBlue, Havlak 4.31 vs 10.24, NBody, Richards, Sieve 1.62 vs 3.61), and without the Bounce outlier the geomeans are 2.46 vs 2.58, about 1.05x (derived from page data); Node.js has the better median. Its clear AWFY win is over other Rubies: JRuby 12.83 and MRI 45.62. kostya/benchmarks (https://github.com/kostya/benchmarks, update 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G): on bench.b, truffleruby 34.0.1 native 5.169 s and JVM 4.645 s beat Lua/luajit 5.686 s and Python/pypy 9.398 s (Node.js 2.954 s is faster). On the other shared tests it is slower: mandel.b 48.381 s vs luajit 31.804 s and pypy 41.153 s; Json 10.618 s vs pypy 0.606 s; Matmul 17.667 s vs pypy 3.263 s; Primes 0.871 s vs luajit 0.309 s and pypy 0.617 s. On Base64 the JVM mode ties PyPy (3.505 s vs 3.534 s). kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X): truffleruby 22.3.1 in JVM mode beats PyPy3 7.3.11 on 6 of 13 benchmarks and LuaJIT 2.1.0-beta3 on 5 of 11, for example binarytrees 0.69 s vs 3.84 s (PyPy) and 6.73 s (LuaJIT), and nbody 0.85 s vs 4.44 s and 1.44 s.
compiler_and_flags: TruffleRuby 34.0.1 native and JVM release tarballs vs CRuby 4.0.6 built with CC=clang ./configure --enable-yjit (docker/Dockerfile); scripts run via `truffleruby`, `ruby`, `ruby --jit`.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid) per README Environment section; base image and interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile
tradeoffs: Needs warm-up and much more memory (bench.b: 197.19 + 693.00 MiB vs 12.12 + 0.00 MiB for CRuby in the kostya tables). README offers two configurations: Native (faster startup) and JVM (better peak performance).
caveats: Mixed against every listed baseline. On AWFY the geomean edge over Node.js comes mostly from Node's Bounce outlier, and Node.js has the better median. On kostya/benchmarks TruffleRuby is slower than LuaJIT and PyPy on 4 of the 6 shared tests (mandel.b, Json, Matmul, Primes), with Matmul 5.4x and Json 17x slower than PyPy. Node.js beats it on every kostya test shown. On kostya/jit-benchmarks 2023 it wins about half the time. AWFY numbers date from 2016, and the paper is co-authored by Benoit Daloze, a TruffleRuby developer, so it is peer-reviewed but not independent. JVM mode has high memory use (about 350 MB base RSS on kostya). plb2 (https://github.com/attractivechaos/plb2) lists Ruby only on the proprietary 'Graal EE 23.1.1' build. The README claim ('fastest Ruby implementation', yjit-bench) compares against other Rubies, not the listed baselines.

name: Cython
baseline: CPython 3.10.7 (kostya/jit-benchmarks 'Python3' rows; Ubuntu 22.10 package, version listed in the README Versions table)
workload: kostya/jit-benchmarks: benchmarks-game programs (binarytrees, fannkuchredux, mandelbrot, nbody, matmul and others) run as CPython scripts and as Cython-compiled .pyx files.
claimed_speedup: Cython vs Python3 (CPython 3.10.7) best times, round 1 (2023-02-28): binarytrees 0.81 s vs 73.15 s; fannkuchredux 0.13 s vs 4.04 s; mandelbrot 0.43 s vs 37.52 s; nbody 0.56 s vs 53.72 s; matmul 0.39 s vs 22.73 s; spectralnorm 0.11 s vs 20.69 s; pidigits 1.73 s vs 6.17 s (about 31x to 188x on the numeric kernels, derived from page data). Small or no win on text tests: fasta 6.81 s vs 8.65 s, knucleotide 8.33 s vs 8.41 s; slower on regexdna 6.1 s vs 5.2 s; brainfuck 165.97 s vs CPython timing out above 190 s. No Cython row for brainfuck2 or revcomp.
compiler_and_flags: Cython 0.29.30 (Ubuntu cython3 package) `cython3 --embed test.pyx`, then gcc (Ubuntu 22.10 build-essential; the suite reports gcc 12.2.0) `-O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -Wno-unused-result -g`, linked with -lpython3.10 (tools/languages.rb, GCC_FLAGS and the cython build_cmd).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10 (README, round 1 dated 2023-02-28)
stars_or_usage: 10.9k stars; README cites more than 70 million PyPI downloads per month
tradeoffs: Needs a build step and a C/C++ compiler; the large speedups require cdef type annotations and C-level constructs, i.e. effectively a different (typed) program. Output can be C++ and linked from C++ code.
caveats: The .pyx files are hand-typed Cython that is close to C: binarytrees allocates C structs with malloc/free while the CPython test.py builds Python class instances, and nbody uses cdef structs and extern math.h (Cythonized by Robert Bradshaw), so the numbers measure statically typed Cython, not unmodified Python compiled by Cython. Several CPython rows are a single run (binarytrees, nbody). Time is measured inside the program with time.time(), so process start-up and the 0.8-2.6 s Cython+gcc compile time are excluded. Versions are old (Cython 0.29.30, Python 3.10.7, round 1 dated 2023-02-28, not rerun). Cython's own README makes no numeric speed claim. Cython is a Python-to-C compiler rather than an interpreter.

name: GraalPy
baseline: CPython (first-party: CPython 3.12.8; independent suite: CPython 3.10.7); PyPy3 7.3.11 also in the independent suite, where GraalPy mostly loses
workload: Benchmarks Game style single-threaded programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, fannkuchredux, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, matmul, nbody, pidigits, regexdna, revcomp, spectralnorm) run as whole processes in kostya/jit-benchmarks; first-party: pyperformance geomean over the pair-wise intersection of working benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Independent kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (GraalPy 22.3.1 '--jvm' vs CPython 3.10.7, best time in s): binarytrees 2.02 vs 73.15, fannkuchredux 0.36 vs 4.04, fasta 3.53 vs 8.65, knucleotide 5.04 vs 8.41, mandelbrot 0.84 vs 37.52, matmul 1.4 vs 22.73, nbody 3.19 vs 53.72, spectralnorm 0.62 vs 20.69, brainfuck2 11.44 vs 142.26, brainfuck 14.22 vs >190 (CPython timed out); slower than CPython on pidigits 9.78 vs 6.17, regexdna 9.04 vs 5.2, revcomp 4.36 vs 2.45. Against PyPy3 7.3.11 GraalPy wins only 4 of 13 (binarytrees 2.02 vs 3.84, fannkuchredux 0.36 vs 0.71, nbody 3.19 vs 4.44, spectralnorm 0.62 vs 0.71) and loses 9 (e.g. brainfuck 14.22 vs 8.77, matmul 1.4 vs 0.36, mandelbrot 0.84 vs 0.54, regexdna 9.04 vs 2.38). First-party: GraalPy 25.1.3 geomean 4.30x faster than CPython 3.12.8 on pyperformance when JIT compiled (README '~4x', docs/user/assets/performance.svg); without the Graal JIT about 4x slower than CPython (docs/user/Performance.md).
compiler_and_flags: Independent suite: GraalVM image with 'gu install python', run as 'graalpython --jvm <file>' (GraalPy 22.3.1, Python 3.8.5); CPython 3.10.7 from Ubuntu 22.10 apt; PyPy3 7.3.11 official linux64 tarball; Docker on Ubuntu 22.10. First-party: each interpreter installed via pyenv, 'pyperformance run', flags and JDK not stated.
hardware: Independent suite: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10. First-party page states no hardware.
tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM and needs JIT warm-up; README describes native extension module support as experimental.
caveats: Java implementation (runs on the JVM or as a GraalVM native image), not a C++ library; listed because the claim is against Python implementations and its JIT is the Graal compiler. Independent numbers are for GraalPy 22.3.1 (Feb 2023), not the current release; whole-process times, so JVM startup and JIT warm-up are included. Against PyPy, the jits-category incumbent, GraalPy loses 9 of 13 benchmarks. Memory is far higher: 1.1-3.3 GB max RSS for GraalPy JVM vs 8-951 MB for CPython in the suite (binarytrees 3265 MB vs 98.5 MB). Without JIT compilation GraalPy is about 4x slower than CPython, so short scripts are slower; C-extension-heavy code benefits little. First-party 4x geomean has no hardware and only covers benchmarks that run on both.

name: CPython tail-calling interpreter
baseline: CPython computed-goto interpreter loop (same source, default dispatch)
workload: pyperformance suite, CPython built with clang-19, ThinLTO and PGO on AMD64 Ubuntu 22.04; per-benchmark results in gist https://gist.github.com/Fidget-Spinner/497c664eef389622d146d632990b0d21 (main 2228e92da31c vs tail-call 465467f47553, 2025-01-05).
claimed_speedup: After correction: geomean 3-5% faster on pyperformance (issue correction notice; Python 3.14 What's New says 3-5% depending on platform and architecture, baseline Python 3.14 built with Clang 19 without the new interpreter). The original claim of 10% geomean, up to 40% on Python-heavy benchmarks (gist: 1.10x geomean, best 1.46x on scimark_sor, unpickle_list 1.02x slower) was artificially boosted by an LLVM 19 bug that slowed the computed-goto baseline.
compiler_and_flags: clang-19 (needs Clang 19+ on x86-64 and AArch64), ThinLTO and PGO; PGO is said to be especially crucial for the speedup.
hardware: AMD64 machine, Ubuntu 22.04 (CPU model not on the page)
tradeoffs: Needs Clang 19 or newer (x86-64 and AArch64) and PGO to pay off per the issue.
caveats: Baseline is CPython itself, so this is a delta against the incumbent's previous dispatch, not against another implementation. The headline 10%/40% numbers were withdrawn by the authors after an LLVM 19 bug was found; the corrected 3-5% geomean is the figure to use, and even that baseline is the Clang 19 computed-goto build, which issue #158283 measures as 7.7% slower than a GCC 13 build on Linux x86-64 and 11.4% slower with Xcode 16.4 on macOS arm64 (merged dispatch jumps). An independent measurement by Nelson Elhage (blog.nelhage.com, snippet only, blocked here) found only 1.03x on a Raptor Lake i5-13500 and 1.00x on an Apple M1 against a clang-18 computed-goto build. Needs Clang 19+ on x86-64/AArch64 and PGO; opt-in via --with-tail-call-interp. Separately, Python 3.15 What's New reports 15-20% pyperformance geomean on Windows x86-64 with MSVC 18 (Visual Studio 18.1.1) versus the switch-case interpreter on an AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (chart in faster-cpython/ideas results/5800X-msvc.pgo2-vs-msvc.pgo.tc.svg), and the official Windows 64-bit binaries now use the tail-calling interpreter. CPU model absent for the clang claim, so the tier is C.

name: Dino
baseline: Python 3.4.x and Ruby 2.1.x (also PyPy 2.2.x, SpiderMonkey 1.8.x, Scala 2.10.x, OCaml 4.0.x)
workload: Old computer-language-shootout style programs (loop, hash, fact, fib, exceptions, method calls, object creation, sieve, sort, statistics, random, threads, startup, compile) on x86-64, AARCH64, ARM and PPC64; times are relative to Dino's best result = 1.0.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 (relative times, Dino best = 1.0; plain Dino without hints / Python / Ruby): Loop 19 / 257 / 157; Fact 13.2 / 90.4 / 25.2; Fib 112 / 492 / 142; Method 1.0 / 5.8 / 1.5; Object 1.0 / 4.4 / 1.4; Sieve 1.0 / 37.9 / 4.5; Thread 1.0 / 125 / 43.6; Start 1.0 / 10.9 / 29.4; Hash 1.0 / 2.4 / 2.2. PyPy beats plain Dino on loop (8.1 vs 19), hash (0.4), fact (0.4 vs 13.2), fib (59 vs 112), except (0.4), method (0.2), object (0.1) and random (0.9 vs 3.1), and beats even Dino's best hinted row on hash, fact, except, method, object and random.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated.
hardware: x86-64 i5-4670 3.4 GHz Haswell; also AARCH64 (X-Gene), ARM (Exynos 5410 1.6 GHz Cortex-A15), PPC64 (3.5 GHz Power7)
license: GPL-2.0-or-later (DINO interpreter sources; COPYING is GPLv2) and LGPL-2.0-or-later (AMMUNITION library sources; COPYING.LIB is the Library GPL v2)
tradeoffs: Dynamically typed scripting language with an optimizing bytecode interpreter, mark-and-sweep plus mark-and-copy GC, optional function-level JIT through C code generation, type inference, fibers and a C FFI; its own language, not source compatible with Python or Ruby.
caveats: Results are from a 2016 README slide deck (version 0.98 development) on Python 3.4 and Ruby 2.1; numbers are relative to Dino's best run, not seconds. Dino's best row uses JIT, pure-function and inline hints; the plain row is quoted here. PyPy is faster than plain Dino on 8 of 14 benchmarks on x86-64. On AARCH64 Python 2.7.5 was used (Python 3 absent) and Python wins hash (0.5 vs 1.7); on ARM Python beats plain Dino on fact (4.4 vs 18.1) and hash (0.6 vs 1.0); on PPC64 Ruby beats plain Dino on loop (17.6 vs 23.2). The thread benchmark compares Dino green threads with GIL-bound OS threads. The benchmark driver is DINO/compare.tst (shell script, old shootout programs); compiler version and flags for the interpreter build are not stated. The companion arXiv preprint (dino.pdf in dino-lang/implemenation-article, dated 2016/4/5) has a variant table on Python 3.3.x and Ruby 2.0.x with different numbers (e.g. x86-64 loop Python 416, Ruby 237), Fedora Core 21, and GCC 4.9.2 used only for JIT compilation. Author is a GCC maintainer; repo dormant since 2019-11-19.
found_via: Recalled Vladimir Makarov's Dino (he also wrote MIR, which is already catalogued) while checking interpreter READMEs; opened github.com/dino-lang/dino, its raw README.md and commit feed.

name: KPHP
baseline: PHP 7.4 with OpCache (Zend micro_bench.php and bench.php); PHP 7.2 for the vk.com page timings
workload: php-src Zend/micro_bench.php and Zend/bench.php (after removing a couple of tests that do not compile), 5 runs each; plus vk.com page generation times and ML-style kernels measured by the authors.
claimed_speedup: micro_bench avg 3.297 s on PHP 7.4 vs 0.460 s on KPHP; bench avg 0.659 s vs 0.119 s ('KPHP is found to be 5-7 times faster'); vk.com/feed 10.1 s vs 0.95 s, vk.com/im 1.25 s vs 0.46 s, vk.com/ads 0.73 s vs 0.20 s (PHP 7.2); neural networks with huge matrices ~8 s vs 0.24 s; deep decision trees ~5 s vs 0.14 s; README: 'when your code fits best practices, it runs 3-10 times faster than PHP'. Companion walk-through page (docs/various-topics/walk-through-php-kphp-cpp.md, quicksort of an int array): PHP 7.4 ~2100 ms vs KPHP ~480 ms (~4x); with the array_swap_int_keys built-in and no wrapper call, PHP 7.4 ~1950 ms vs KPHP ~270 ms (~7x); hand-written C++ with g++ -Os ~220 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the Zend runs (PHP 7.4 with OpCache and without XDebug; KPHP version and CPU not given). The walk-through page says KPHP builds its generated C++ with g++ at -Os.
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time compiler from a limited, strictly typed PHP subset to C++ and then a native binary; no generators, anonymous classes, SPL or XML parsing, no call-by-name; existing PHP code usually needs rewriting to compile; the runtime is C++ and has a fast FFI.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model or KPHP/compiler version. The Zend micro_bench.php and bench.php had a couple of tests removed and errors corrected before running, and the modified scripts are not published. The doc itself calls the Zend comparison 'absolutely synthetic' and warns it is wrong to say KPHP is always faster (code dominated by C-implemented PHP functions such as strpos or parse_url gains almost nothing). The walk-through shows KPHP dropping to ~940 ms when types degrade to mixed[], and hand-written C++ still about 2x faster than plain KPHP. Baseline is PHP 7.4/7.2, without the PHP 8 JIT, so today's gap is probably smaller. vk.com page timings and ML kernels are not reproducible from public code. KPHP only compiles a restricted, strictly typed PHP subset (no generators, anonymous classes, SPL or XML), so existing code usually needs rewriting. The project website is on github.io (blocked here); pages were read from the repo's docs/ directory.

name: LLRT (Low Latency Runtime)
baseline: Node.js 20 (V8) on AWS Lambda
workload: AWS Lambda DynamoDB Put function (example/functions/src/v3-lib.mjs), ARM, 128MB: 64 cold starts and 20000 warm starts, percentiles p0-p100 of Lambda-reported Init Duration plus Function Duration and of HTTP round-trip time; results only as two PNG screenshots in the README.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'up to over 10x faster startup and up to 2x overall lower cost compared to other JavaScript runtimes running on AWS Lambda'. Screenshots (benchmarks/llrt-ddb-put.png vs benchmarks/node20-ddb-put.png, DynamoDB Put, ARM, 128MB, 64 cold starts, 20000 warm starts): cold-start p50 Lambda-reported Init+Function duration 64.16 ms vs 1511.93 ms for Node.js 20 (about 23.6x, derived from page data); cold-start p50 HTTP round trip 235.61 ms vs 1719.00 ms (about 7.3x, derived from page data); warm p50 14.94 vs 33.20 ms (lambda) and 43.72 vs 62.08 ms (HTTP). The 2x cost claim has no numbers on the page.
hardware: AWS Lambda ARM, 128MB memory (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: No JIT, so peak compute is far slower than V8 and not recommended for compute-heavy work; partial Node.js API compatibility; ES2023 only; README marks it experimental and for evaluation purposes.

name: LuaAOT (lua-aot-5.4)
baseline: Lua 5.4.3 interpreter (the stock interpreter the fork is based on)
workload: Seven Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs in experiments/ (binarytrees, fannkuch, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, nbody, spectralnorm) compiled ahead of time to C with luaot and run through experiments/main.lua, versus the same scripts on the stock Lua 5.4.3 interpreter and LuaJIT; 20 runs each, wall-clock time.
claimed_speedup: README: 'For numerical benchmarks it can be twice as fast as regular Lua. But overall, it is not as fast as LuaJIT or Pallene.' Repo statistics/times-slow.txt (mean wall time of 20 runs, LuaAOT vs Lua 5.4.3 interpreter, derived from page data): binarytrees 2.68 s vs 3.51 s (1.31x), fannkuch 21.92 vs 44.31 s (2.02x), fasta 3.84 vs 5.05 s (1.32x), knucleotide 3.44 vs 4.15 s (1.21x), mandelbrot 6.17 vs 16.27 s (2.64x), nbody 12.14 vs 18.23 s (1.50x), spectralnorm 19.00 vs 39.86 s (2.10x). LuaJIT on the same runs was 2.4x to 31x faster than Lua. SBLP 2021 paper abstract: LuaAOT reduced benchmark running times by 20% to 60% (snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: Interpreter built with the Lua 5.4.3 Makefile (gcc -std=gnu99 -O2, make guess); benchmark modules compiled with gcc -shared -fPIC -O2 -g (scripts/compile). gcc version not stated.
tradeoffs: Modified Lua 5.4.3 with an extra luaot compiler that translates Lua bytecode to C (jumps become gotos, no bytecode dispatch); keeps full Lua 5.4 semantics and is embeddable from C/C++, but compiled modules must be built per script.
caveats: CPU model and gcc version not stated (perf counters in statistics/perf-slow.txt only show about 3.06 GHz); the timing file is undated and comes from the paper's experiments. The paper itself (ACM DL, inf.puc-rio.br preprint) is blocked here, so its numbers are snippet only. Gains are uneven: 1.21x to 1.5x on four of seven benchmarks, about 2x to 2.6x only on fannkuch, mandelbrot and spectralnorm; LuaJIT is far faster on every benchmark. Based on Lua 5.4.3 (older than 5.4.7/5.5), every module must be compiled to C with a C compiler at build time, and the repo has had no commits since 2023-12-06.

name: Spinel
baseline: CRuby 4.0.4 (MRI interpreter) and CRuby 4.0.4 with --yjit
workload: 28 benchmarks in the repository's benchmark/ directory (mandelbrot, fib, matmul, nqueens, sieve, binary_trees, json_parse, ao_render and others), compiled ahead of time to native executables by Spinel versus the same scripts run by CRuby.
claimed_speedup: 'Geometric mean: ~8.5x faster than Ruby 4.0.4 with --yjit across the 28 benchmarks (~15.2x against the interpreter)'. Examples vs YJIT: mandelbrot 18 ms vs 938 ms (53.6x), matmul 6.1 ms vs 201 ms (32.9x), binary_trees 2.7 ms vs 13 ms (4.7x), json_parse 28 ms vs 133 ms (4.7x), csv_process 95 ms vs 396 ms (4.2x).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3 builds the generated C; the README does not list flags, but Spinel's cc driver defaults to -O2 (src/main.c opt_level "2", Makefile COPT ?= -O2) plus -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -ffp-contract=off. CRuby 4.0.4 (revision b89eb1bc) run with --disable-gems, and with --yjit for the JIT column; each cell is the mean of five wall-clock runs under `perf stat -r 5`, measured 2026-09-17 on spinel 74c8e0a4.
hardware: '32-core Linux box' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: An ahead-of-time compiler for a Ruby subset (see the README Supported Ruby Features section), not a drop-in interpreter: it does whole-program type inference, emits C and invokes the system cc. Compiled binaries start in about 0.8 ms.
caveats: First-party numbers with only a core count for hardware; no timing script is checked in (make bench is a pass/fail output check against CRuby), so the perf stat runs are not reproducible from the repo as-is. Sub-10 ms cells are dominated by process startup (about 0.8 ms per binary; README says those ratios are lower bounds). The README itself warns the fib row (44.6x vs YJIT) reflects the C compiler folding a pure call tree at build time, not per-call speed. YJIT is essentially identical to the interpreter on mandelbrot, nqueens, matmul, partial_sums and sieve, so the largest multiples there are against an un-accelerated baseline. Spinel compiles a Ruby subset (whole-program type inference, no eval or dynamic metaprogramming), so the benchmarks are programs inside that subset. The geometric means (8.5x vs YJIT, 15.2x vs interpreter) reproduce from the 28 table rows (derived from page data).

name: Wren
baseline: Lua 5.2.3, Python 3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0p247 (also Python 2.7.5 and LuaJIT 2.0.2 with JIT off)
workload: Four small benchmarks (method call, DeltaBlue, binary trees, recursive Fibonacci); best of 10 runs, interpreter startup excluded.
claimed_speedup: Method call: wren 0.12 s vs luajit -joff 0.16 s, ruby 0.20 s, lua 0.35 s, python3 0.78 s, python 0.85 s. DeltaBlue: wren 0.13 s vs python3 0.48 s, python 0.57 s (no Lua or Ruby row). Binary trees: luajit -joff 0.11 s, wren 0.22 s, ruby 0.24 s, python 0.37 s, python3 0.38 s, lua 0.52 s. Recursive Fibonacci: luajit -joff 0.10 s, wren 0.20 s, ruby 0.22 s, lua 0.28 s, python 0.51 s, python3 0.57 s. Against Lua 5.2.3 that is about 2.9x, 2.4x and 1.4x faster on method call, binary trees and Fibonacci (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated.
hardware: MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7 (CPU model not named), 16 GB 1,600 MHz DDR3 (author's laptop)
tradeoffs: Small class-based language (VM under 4,000 lines); NaN-tagged values, fixed object layout, copy-down inheritance; classes cannot be modified at runtime; compiles as C99 or C++98 and later, embeddable through a C API.
caveats: Old first-party numbers (undated page; baselines are Lua 5.2.3, LuaJIT 2.0.2, Python 2.7.5/3.3.4 and Ruby 2.0.0, i.e. about 2014) on the author's laptop with no compiler, flags or CPU model stated; modern Lua 5.4, CPython 3.11+ and Ruby 3.x are faster, so the margins are likely smaller today. LuaJIT in interpreter mode (-joff) beats Wren on binary trees (0.11 s vs 0.22 s) and Fibonacci (0.10 s vs 0.20 s); DeltaBlue is compared only with Python. Development is slow: the 2025-11-19 commits are a merged PR (#1194, method-limit checks) plus CI edits, and the previous commits are from 2025-03.

name: YJIT (CRuby)
baseline: CRuby 4.1.0dev bytecode interpreter (same commit, JIT off); the report also shows CRuby 3.4.7 and YJIT 3.4.7
workload: ruby-bench (commit 17dcac94) on Ruby master 11bb12ad3c, 2026-09-20: 16 headline benchmarks (activerecord, chunky-png, erubi-rails, hexapdf, liquid-c, liquid-compile, liquid-il, liquid-render, lobsters, mail, psych-load, railsbench, rubocop, ruby-lsp, sequel, shipit) plus about 60 other and micro benchmarks; 5 warmup iterations for the interpreter and 50 for YJIT before timing.
claimed_speedup: x86_64 (Xeon Platinum 8488C): geomean of the headline benchmarks, YJIT 4.1.0dev is 99.2% faster than CRuby 4.1.0dev and 9.5% faster than YJIT 3.4.7; railsbench 120.1% faster than the interpreter. Per-benchmark interpreter/YJIT time from the x86_64 CSV (derived from page data): activerecord 2.76x, liquid-render 2.89x, railsbench 2.20x, optcarrot 3.79x, lee 1.95x, binarytrees 2.31x, nbody 2.59x, fannkuchredux 4.04x, fib 6.58x, 30k_ifelse 7.62x, 30k_methods 11.84x; 78 of 79 benchmarks faster, knucleotide 0.98x. aarch64 (Graviton4): headline geomean 1.73x, railsbench 1.87x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Ubuntu 14.3.0-12ubuntu1~24~ppa1) 14.3.0; Ruby configured with --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc --enable-yjit --enable-zjit (default optimization flags); YJIT enabled at run time with --yjit; rustc version not stated.
hardware: x86_64: Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C; aarch64: AWS Graviton4
stars_or_usage: Ships in CRuby (ruby/ruby 23.8k stars); the sibling ZJIT is in the same repository
tradeoffs: Uses more memory than the interpreter (executable memory plus metadata); supported on x86-64 and arm64/aarch64 macOS, Linux and BSD; requires a Rust toolchain to build; warmup needed.
caveats: Run by the YJIT team at Shopify (first-party), though code, Ruby commit, build config and CPU are all published and raw per-benchmark CSVs are in rubybench/yjit-reports. Speedups are after warmup (50 YJIT warmup iterations); first-iteration and memory costs differ: YJIT uses more memory than the interpreter on most headline benchmarks (memory chart on the same report). The large micro-benchmark ratios (30k_methods 11.8x, fib 6.6x) do not carry over to applications, where the headline geomean is about 2x on x86_64 and 1.7x on Graviton4. The repository is all of CRuby, so stars and license describe CRuby; YJIT is the yjit/ directory. The VMIL 2021 and MPLR 2023 papers were not opened (dl.acm.org blocked). speed.ruby-lang.org itself was blocked here; its numbers were read from the generated HTML and CSV in rubybench/yjit-reports (branch pages).
